        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "The Moon’s orbital period would increase by a factor of 2 \\sqrt{2}. Kepler’s third law of orbital bodies states that their orbital periods squared are proportional to their orbital radius cubed:</p> T^2 \\propto R^3 \\implies \\left(\\frac{T_{\\text{new}}}{T_{\\text{old}}}\\right)^2 = \\left(\\frac{R_{\\text{new}}}{R_{\\text{old}}}\\right)^3 $$\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Substituting $R_{new}$ = 2$R_{old}$:</p> \\left(\\frac{T_{\\text{new}}}{T_{\\text{old}}}\\right)^2 = 2^3 = 8  \r\n<p class=\"exp\">Cancel $R$ and solve for $T_{new}$:</p> T_{\\text{new}} = \\sqrt{8}\\,T_{\\text{old}} = 2\\sqrt{2}\\,T_{\\text{old}}  \r\n<p class=\"exp\">Note that you can also obtain this result by examining the equation for orbital speed from Newton ($v$ = (<i>Gm</i>/$r$)<sup>½</sup>). This shows that the orbital speed of the Moon must decrease by the square root of 2. Coupling this with the knowledge that the new orbit is now twice as large, it will take 2(2<sup>½</sup>) or 2 \\sqrt{2} times as long to orbit once around Earth as it used to.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_12",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "If you went to another planet, which of the following would be true?</p>",
        "options": [
          "Your mass would be the same, but your weight would change.",
          "Your mass would change, but your weight would be the same.",
          "Your mass would be the same, and your weight would be the same.",
          "Your mass would change, and your weight would change."
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "Your mass would be the same, but your weight would change. Mass is a property of an object and measures the object’s inertia regardless of location. Weight is a force due to gravity and depends both on the object’s mass and on the planetary gravity the object is currently experiencing.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_13",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "You lift a heavy suitcase twice. Each time you lift it to the same height, but the second time you do it in half the time. Compare the work done to and power delivered to the suitcase.</p>",
        "options": [
          "Same work, same power",
          "Twice the work, twice the power",
          "Twice the work, same power",
          "Same work, twice the power"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Same work, twice the power.</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">Work = force × distance</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">For lifting operations, the force is assumed to be equal to the weight of the object for most of the lift. (Briefly, at the beginning of the lift, the lifting force must be greater than the weight in order to get the object moving. This brief force must be different in the second case in order to get the suitcase moving faster. However, this initial force is generally ignored in these calculations as it does not happen over an appreciable distance, just as the decrease in lifting force at the end of the lift is likewise ignored.) The same force over the same distance yields the same work. If the details of the forces contributing to the work are troublesome, you may prefer to think about the energy gained by the suitcase ($W$ = Δ$E$). Since the suitcase has gained the same amount of energy in both cases by being lifted, the work done must likewise be the same:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">Power = work/time</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">If the same work is done in half the time, twice the power must be supplied.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_14",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "A constant horizontal force of 12 N is applied for 5 meters to move an initially stationary mass of 5 kg. The friction between the floor and the mass does a total of −40 joules of work to the mass. The final speed (in m/s) of the object is</p>",
        "options": [
          "2(6)<sup>½</sup>",
          "2(2)<sup>½</sup>",
          "2(10)<sup>½</sup>",
          "4"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "2(2)<sup>½</sup> m/s. From the work-energy theorem:</p> W_{\\text{net}} = \\Delta KE = F \\cdot d = (10\\text{ N})(2\\text{ m}) = 20\\text{ J} $$\r\n<p class=\"exp\">So the kinetic energy of the mass has gone up by 20 J. Initially, it had no <i>KE</i> since it was stationary. Therefore:</p> KE = \\frac{1}{2}mv^2 \\implies 20 = \\frac{1}{2}(5)v^2 \\implies v = \\sqrt{8} = 2\\sqrt{2}\\text{ m/s} $$</li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_15",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "A skier begins a downhill run at a height of 9 meters and a speed of 2 m/s. If you ignore friction, what will be her speed when she is 3 meters from the bottom of the slope?</p>",
        "options": [
          "6.0 m/s",
          "12.8 m/s",
          "11.1 m/s",
          "7.7 m/s"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "11.1 m/s. Mechanical energy is conserved since there are no nonconservative forces involved:</p> mgh_i + \\frac{1}{2}mv_i^2 = mgh_f + \\frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 $$\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Canceling mass in every term and solving for <i>$v_{f}$</i> yields:</p> v_f = \\sqrt{v_i^2 + 2g(h_i - h_f)} $$</li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_16",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "A rubber ball ($m$ = 0.250 kg) strikes a wall horizontally at 3.50 m/s and rebounds elastically. What is the magnitude of impulse delivered to the wall in N ⋅ s?</p>",
        "options": [
          "0.875",
          "1.75",
          "2.50",
          "8.75"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "1.75</p> \\Delta p = m(v_f - v_i) = (0.05\\text{ kg})(-20 - 15) = -1.75\\text{ kg}\\cdot\\text{m/s} $$\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Since the collision is elastic, no kinetic energy is lost. Assuming the wall remains stationary, the rubber ball must rebound with the same speed but in the opposite direction:</p> v_f = -v_i  \r\n<p class=\"exp\">Substituting for $v$<sub>$f$</sub> above:</p> J = \\Delta p = -1.75\\text{ N}\\cdot\\text{s} \\implies |J| = 1.75\\text{ N}\\cdot\\text{s}  \r\n<p class=\"exp\">Here the negative sign indicates that the impulse delivered to the ball is in the opposite direction from the ball’s initial velocity. Note the ball and the wall receive equal and opposite impulses (from Newton’s third law) and the problem asks for magnitude (absolute value).</p>\r\n<p class=\"expt\">Since $F$Δ$t$ is also an impulse, units of N ⋅ s must be the same as kg ⋅ m/s and is quickly shown:</p> 1\\text{ N}\\cdot\\text{s} = 1(\\text{kg}\\cdot\\text{m/s}^2)\\cdot\\text{s} = 1\\text{ kg}\\cdot\\text{m/s} $$</li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_17",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "A running back ($m$ = 85 kg) running at 1.5 m/s is tackled from the side by another player ($m$ = 75 kg) running perpendicularly to the running back’s original heading at 1.75 m/s. What is the resulting speed of the two entangled players just after the tackle?</p>",
        "options": [
          "2.2 m/s",
          "0.25 m/s",
          "1.6 m/s",
          "1.1 m/s"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "1.1 m/s. Total momentum must be conserved through the collision. So we need to find only the magnitude of the initial momentum of the system. Each player is originally running perpendicularly to the other. Thus, their individual momentums are different components. Imagine one as an $x$-component and the other as a $y$-component. Therefore, the resulting magnitude is found using the Pythagorean theorem. Dividing by total mass yields the speed of the combined players after impact:</p> v_f = \\frac{m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \\frac{(80)(6) + (100)(-4)}{80 + 100} = \\frac{80}{180} = 0.44\\text{ m/s} $$</li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_18",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "Which of the following ranks the torques applied by the three equal forces <i>A, B,</i> and $C$ to the long thin rod about its fixed axis as indicated above?</p>",
        "options": [
          "τ <sub>$C$</sub> &gt; τ <sub>$B$</sub> &gt; τ <sub>$A$</sub>",
          "τ <sub>$A$</sub> = τ <sub>$B$</sub> &gt; τ <sub>$C$</sub>",
          "τ <sub>$B$</sub> = τ <sub>$C$</sub> &gt; τ <sub>$A$</sub>",
          "τ <sub>$B$</sub> &gt; τ <sub>$A$</sub> &gt; τ <sub>$C$</sub>"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "$\\tau$<sub>$B$</sub> &gt; $\\tau$<sub>$A$</sub> &gt; $\\tau$ <sub>$C$</sub></p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">Torque = (force) (distance from axis of rotation) sin θ</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Force $C$ is applied along the lever arm. So force $C$ has an angle of 180°, resulting in no torque.</p> \\tau_C = r F \\sin(180^\\circ) = 0  \r\n<p class=\"exp\">Force $A$ has a much shorter lever arm than force $B$. Therefore, the torque supplied by $A$ is much less than the torque supplied by $B$.</p> \\tau_A = r_A F_A \\sin(90^\\circ) < \\tau_B = r_B F_B \\sin(90^\\circ) $$</li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_19",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "A large spherical cloud of dust in deep space that is spinning slowly collapses under its own gravitational force into a spherical cloud 10 times smaller in diameter. How does its rotational speed change?</p>",
        "options": [
          "The rotational speed does not change.",
          "The rotational speed increases by a factor of 10.",
          "The rotational speed decreases by a factor of 10.",
          "The rotational speed increases by a factor of 100."
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "The rotational speed increases by a factor of 100. The rotational inertia ($I$) for a sphere is proportional to $R^{2}$. Because the shape of the cloud is not changing, we can determine that the rotational inertia has decreased by a factor of 10<sup>2</sup>. Since angular momentum is conserved:</p> L_1 = L_2 \\implies I_1 \\omega_1 = I_2 \\omega_2  \r\n<p class=\"exp\">The new angular velocity ($ω_{2}$) must be 100 times bigger:</p> \\omega_2 = \\frac{I_1}{I_2}\\omega_1 = 100\\,\\omega_1 $$</li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_20",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "Two cars approach an intersection at right angles, as pictured above. What is their relative speed to each other?</p>",
        "options": [
          "10 mph",
          "45 mph",
          "57 mph",
          "80 mph"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "57 mph. Relative velocity is the difference in the velocity vectors. When the vectors are subtracted, the resultant is the hypotenuse of a right triangle:</p> |\\Delta\\vec{v}| = \\sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = \\sqrt{10^2 + 10^2} = 10\\sqrt{2}\\text{ m/s} \\approx 14.1\\text{ m/s} $$</li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "dphys1_21",
        "topic": "Comprehensive AP Physics 1",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "A container of water (pictured below) has two holes in its side allowing two streams of water to emerge as shown. Initially, the lower hole is twice as deep as the higher hole. Which statement best compares the initial velocities of these two streams of water?</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\"><img alt=\"\" class=\"w34\" role=\"presentation\" src=\"images/f020-02.jpg\"/></p>",
        "options": [
          "They emerge at the same speed.",
          "The lower stream emerges 2½ times as fast as the upper stream.",
          "The lower stream emerges 2 times as fast as the upper stream.",
          "The lower stream emerges 4 times as fast as the upper stream."
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "According to Bernoulli’s equation, the square of the velocity of fluid relates to the depth of the fluid, assuming the pressure is the same. (This occurs since the streams of water are released into equal atmospheric pressure and is also known as Torricelli’s theorem.) Comparing the surface of the water to one of the streams:</p> P_1 + \\rho g h_1 + \\frac{1}{2}\\rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \\rho g h_2 + \\frac{1}{2}\\rho v_2^2 $$\r\n<p class=\"exp\">With $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ being equal and the surface being stationary ($v_{1}$ = 0), we are left with:</p> \\rho g h_1 = \\rho g h_2 + \\frac{1}{2}\\rho v_2^2  \r\n<p class=\"exp\">Eliminating and rearranging gives:</p> v_2 = \\sqrt{2g(h_1 - h_2)} $$\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Since the lower hole is twice as deep, the quantity in parentheses will be twice as great for the lower hole as compared with the first. To compare velocities, take the square root of both sides.</p></li>\r\n</ol>\r\n</section>\r\n</section>\r\n<section>"
      },

  "ap-topic-calc-ab-test1": {
    "id": "ap-topic-calc-ab-test1",
    "title": "AP Calculus AB: Topic Practice Test 1",
    "subject": "AP Calculus AB",
    "category": "Math & CS",
    "level": "Topic Test",
    "timeLimitMinutes": 40,
    "questionsCount": 20,
    "questions": [
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_1",
        "topic": "Limits",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Evaluate: $\\lim_{x \\to 2} \\frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$",
        "options": [
          "0",
          "2",
          "4",
          "Does not exist"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "Factor $x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)$. The expression simplifies to $x + 2$, so as $x \\to 2$, the limit is \\$2 + 2 = 4$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_2",
        "topic": "Continuity",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "For which value of $k$ is $f(x)$ continuous at $x = 3$? <br>$f(x) = \\begin{cases} x^2 + k, & x < 3 \\\\ 12, & x \\ge 3 \\end{cases}$",
        "options": [
          "2",
          "3",
          "4",
          "6"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "For continuity at $x = 3$, $\\lim_{x \\to 3^-} f(x) = f(3)$. Thus, \\$3^2 + k = 12 \\implies 9 + k = 12 \\implies k = 3$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_3",
        "topic": "Derivatives",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "If $f(x) = x^2$, then $f'(3)$ is:",
        "options": [
          "3",
          "6",
          "9",
          "12"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "$f'(x) = 2x$, so $f'(3) = 2(3) = 6$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_4",
        "topic": "Power Rule",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "If $f(x) = 5x^4 - 3x^2 + 7$, then $f'(x)$ is:",
        "options": [
          "$20x^3 -6x$",
          "$20x^4 -6x$",
          "$5x^3 -3x$",
          "$20x^3 -3x$"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "Apply the power rule term-by-term: $\\frac{d}{dx}(5x^4) - \\frac{d}{dx}(3x^2) + \\frac{d}{dx}(7) = 20x^3 $-6x$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_5",
        "topic": "Product Rule",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "Find the derivative of $f(x) = x^2 e^x$:",
        "options": [
          "$2x e^x$",
          "$x^2 e^x$",
          "$e^x (x^2 + 2x)$",
          "$2x + e^x$"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "Using the product rule: $f'(x) = (2x)e^x + x^2 e^x = e^x(x^2 + 2x)$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_6",
        "topic": "Chain Rule",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "Find $\\frac{d}{dx} \\sin(3x^2)$:",
        "options": [
          "$\\cos(3x^2)$",
          "$6x \\cos(3x^2)$",
          "$3x \\cos(3x^2)$",
          "$6x \\sin(3x^2)$"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "Outer derivative is $\\cos(3x^2)$ and inner derivative is $6x$, so $f'(x) = 6x \\cos(3x^2)$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_7",
        "topic": "Implicit Differentiation",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "Given $x^2 + y^2 = 25$, what is $\\frac{dy}{dx}$?",
        "options": [
          "$\\frac{y}{x}$",
          "$-\\frac{y}{x}$",
          "$\\frac{x}{y}$",
          "$-\\frac{x}{y}$"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Differentiating implicitly: $2x + 2y \\frac{dy}{dx} = 0 \\implies 2y \\frac{dy}{dx} = $-2x$ \\implies \\frac{dy}{dx} = -\\frac{x}{y}$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_8",
        "topic": "Tangent Line",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "For $f(x) = x^2 + 1$, find the equation of the tangent line at $x = 2$.",
        "options": [
          "$y = 4x - 3$",
          "$y = 4x + 3$",
          "$y = 2x + 1$",
          "$y = 4x - 1$"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "$f(2) = 5$, slope $m = f'(2) = 2(2) = 4$. Tangent equation: $y - 5 = 4(x - 2) \\implies y = 4x - 3$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_9",
        "topic": "Related Rates",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "The radius of a circle increases at \\$2 \\text{ cm/s}$. How fast is its area increasing when $r = 3$?",
        "options": [
          "\\$6\\pi$",
          "\\$9\\pi$",
          "\\$12\\pi$",
          "\\$18\\pi$"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "$A = \\pi r^2 \\implies \\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\\pi r \\frac{dr}{dt} = 2\\pi(3)(2) = 12\\pi$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_10",
        "topic": "Critical Points",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "For $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2$, the critical numbers are:",

          "0, 2",
          "1, 2",
          "0, 3",
          "2, 3"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2) = 0 \\implies x = 0, 2$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_11",
        "topic": "Increasing Function",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "For $f(x) = x^3 -3x$, on which interval(s) is $f$ increasing?",
        "options": [
          "$(-1, 1)$",
          "$(-\\infty, -1) \\cup (1, \\infty)$",
          "$(-\\infty, 1)$",
          "$(1, \\infty)$"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1)$. The derivative is positive when $x < -1$ or $x > 1$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_12",
        "topic": "Local Maximum",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "For $f(x) = x^3 -3x$, where does the local maximum occur?",
        "options": [
          "$x = -1$",
          "$x = 0$",
          "$x = 1$",
          "$x = 3$"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "$f'(x) = 3(x+1)(x-1)$ changes sign from positive to negative at $x = -1$, giving a local maximum."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_13",
        "topic": "Concavity",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "For $f(x) = x^3$, where is the function concave down?",
        "options": [
          "$x < 0$",
          "$x > 0$",
          "All real $x$",
          "Nowhere"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "$f''(x) = 6x$. Concave down means $f''(x) < 0$, which holds for $x < 0$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_14",
        "topic": "Mean Value Theorem",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "For $f(x) = x^2$ on $[1, 3]$, what is the value of $c$ guaranteed by MVT?",

          "1",
          "1.5",
          "2",
          "2.5"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "Average rate of change is $\\frac{f(3)$-f$(1)}{3-1} = \\frac{9-1}{2} = 4$. Set $f'(c) = 2c = 4 \\implies c = 2$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_15",
        "topic": "Absolute Maximum",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "On $[0, 3]$, the maximum value of $f(x) = x^2 -2x$ occurs at:",
        "options": [
          "$x = 0$",
          "$x = 1$",
          "$x = 2$",
          "$x = 3$"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Check critical point $f'(x) = 2x-2=0 \\implies x=1$ and endpoints: $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=-1$, $f(3)=3$. Absolute max is at $x = 3$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_16",
        "topic": "Indefinite Integral",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Evaluate: $\\int 3x^2\\,dx$",
        "options": [
          "$x^3 + C$",
          "$3x^3 + C$",
          "$x^2 + C$",
          "$6x + C$"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "Power rule for integrals: $\\int 3x^2 dx = 3 \\cdot \\frac{x^3}{3} + C = x^3  + C$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_17",
        "topic": "Definite Integral",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Evaluate: $\\int_0^2 x\\,dx$",
        "options": [
          "1",
          "2",
          "3",
          "4"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "$\\left[ \\frac{x^2}{2} \\right]_0^2 = \\frac{4}{2} - 0 = 2$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_18",
        "topic": "Fundamental Theorem of Calculus",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "If $F(x) = \\int_1^x (t^3 + 2t) , dt$, then $F'(x)$ equals:",
        "options": [
          "$x^2 + 2$",
          "$x^3 +2x$",
          "$3x^2 + 2$",
          "$x^4 + 2x^2$"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "By FTC Part 1, $F'(x) = \\frac{d}{dx} \\int_1^x (t^3 + 2t) dt = x^3 +2x$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_19",
        "topic": "Area Between Curves",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "The area of the region bounded between $y = x$ and $y = x^2$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 1$ is:",
        "options": [
          "$\\frac{1}{3}$",
          "$\\frac{1}{4}$",
          "$\\frac{1}{6}$",
          "$\\frac{1}{2}$"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "$$\\int_{0}^{1} (x - x^2) dx = $left[ \\frac{x^2}{2} - \\frac{x^3}{3} \\right]_0^1 = \\frac{1}{2} - \\frac{1}{3} = \\frac{1}{6}$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calc_t1_20",
        "topic": "Average Value",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "The average value of $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 2]$ is:",
        "options": [
          "1",
          "$\\frac{4}{3}$",
          "2",
          "$\\frac{8}{3}$"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "$f_{avg} = \\frac{1}{2-0}$\\int_{0}^{2} x^2 dx = $frac{1}{2} \\left[ \\frac{x^3}{3} \\right]_0^2 = \\frac{1}{2} \\cdot \\frac{8}{3} = \\frac{4}{3}$."
      }
    ],
    "testType": "Topic Test"
  },

  "ap-topic-calcbc-test1": {
    "id": "ap-topic-calcbc-test1",
    "title": "AP Calculus BC: Topic Practice Test 1",
    "subject": "AP Calculus BC",
    "category": "Math & CS",
    "level": "Topic Test",
    "timeLimitMinutes": 40,
    "questionsCount": 20,
    "questions": [
      {
        "id": "calcbc_t1_1",
        "topic": "Parametric Derivative",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "Given $x = t^2$ and $y = t^3$, find $\\frac{dy}{dx}$ at $t = 2$.",
        "options": [
          "2",
          "3",
          "4",
          "6"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "$\\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \\frac{3t^2}{2t} = \\frac{3}{2}t$. At $t = 2$, $\\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{3}{2}(2) = 3$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calcbc_t1_2",
        "topic": "Second Derivative Parametric",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "For $x = t^2$ and $y = t^3$, what is $\\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at $t = 2$?",
        "options": [
          "$\\frac{3}{8}$",
          "$\\frac{1}{2}$",
          "$\\frac{3}{4}$",
          "1"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "$\\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{3}{2}t$. Then $\\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \\frac{\\frac{d}{dt}(dy/dx)}{dx/dt} = \\frac{3/2}{2t} = \\frac{3}{4t}$. At $t = 2$, $\\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \\frac{3}{8}$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calcbc_t1_3",
        "topic": "Parametric Tangent",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "For $x = t^2 - 1$ and $y = t^3 - 3t$, a horizontal tangent occurs when:",
        "options": [
          "$t = 0$ only",
          "$t = \\pm 1$",
          "$t = \\pm \\sqrt{3}$",
          "$t = 3$"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "Horizontal tangent occurs when $\\frac{dy}{dt} = 3t^2 - 3 = 0 \\implies t = \\pm 1$ (where $\\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t \\neq 0$)."
      },
      {
        "id": "calcbc_t1_4",
        "topic": "Polar Coordinates",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "For $r = 2$, what is the Cartesian point $(x, y)$ when $\\theta = \\pi/2$?",
        "options": [
          "(2, 0)",
          "(0, 2)",
          "(-2, 0)",
          "(0, -2)"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "$x = r \\cos\\theta = 2 \\cos(\\pi/2) = 0$, $y = r \\sin\\theta = 2 \\sin(\\pi/2) = 2$. Point is $(0, 2)$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calcbc_t1_5",
        "topic": "Polar Area",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "The area enclosed by the polar curve $r = 2$ is:",
        "options": [
          "\\$2\\pi$",
          "\\$4\\pi$",
          "\\$8\\pi$",
          "$\\pi$"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "$A = \\frac{1}{2}$\\int_{0}^{{2\\pi}} r^2 d$theta = \\frac{1}{2}(4)(2\\pi) = 4\\pi$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calcbc_t1_6",
        "topic": "Polar Derivative",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "For $r = 1 + \\cos\\theta$, the derivative $\\frac{dy}{dx}$ is given by:",
        "options": [
          "$\\frac{\\cos\\theta}{\\sin\\theta}$",
          "$\\frac{\\frac{dr}{d\\theta}\\sin\\theta + r\\cos\\theta}{\\frac{dr}{d\\theta}\\cos\\theta - r\\sin\\theta}$",
          "$\\frac{d\\theta}{dr}$",
          "$r \\cos\\theta$"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "Since $y = r\\sin\\theta$ and $x = r\\cos\\theta$, $\\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{dy/d\\theta}{dx/d\\theta} = \\frac{r'\\sin\\theta + r\\cos\\theta}{r'\\cos\\theta - r\\sin\\theta}$."
      },
      {
        "id": "calcbc_t1_7",
        "topic": "Series Convergence",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Determine whether the series $\\sum_{n=1}^\\infty \\frac{1}{n^2}$ converges or diverges.",
        "options": [
          "Converges",
          "Diverges",
          "Oscillates",
          "Cannot determine"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "It is a $p$-series with $p = 2 > 1$, which converges."
      },
      {
        "id": "calcbc_t1_8",
        "topic": "Harmonic Series",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "The harmonic series $\\sum_{n=1}^\\infty \\frac{1}{n}$:",
        "options": [
          "Converges",
          "Diverges",

        "topic": "Kinematics",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "A ball is thrown upward with an initial velocity of 20 m/s. How long will the ball take to reach its maximum height?</p>",
        "options": [
          "19.6 s",
          "9.8 s",
          "6.3 s",
          "2.04 s"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Given the initial velocity of 20 m/s, we know that the ball is decelerated by gravity at a rate of 9.8 m/$s^{2}$. Therefore, we need to know how long gravity will take to decelerate the ball to zero velocity. Clearly, from the definition of acceleration, dividing 20 m/s by 9.8 m/$s^{2}$ gives the answer: 2.04 s.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_kin_2",
        "topic": "Kinematics",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "An airplane lands on a runway with a velocity of 150 m/s. How far will it travel until it stops if its rate of deceleration is constant at −3 m/$s^{2}$?</p>",
        "options": [
          "525 m",
          "3,750 m",
          "6,235 m",
          "9,813 m"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "We do not know the time needed to stop, but we do know that the final velocity is zero. If we use the formula</p> v_y = v_0\\sin\\theta - gt = 40\\sin(30^\\circ) - (9.8)(1) = 20 - 9.8 = 10.2\\text{ m/s} $$\r\n<p class=\"expt\">and substitute 150 m/s for the initial velocity and −3 m/$s^{2}$ for the deceleration, we get the answer: 3,750 m.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },

        "topic": "Kinematics",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "A ball is thrown downward from the top of a roof with a speed of 25 m/s. After 2 s, its velocity will be</p>",
        "options": [
          "19.6 m/s",

          "−44.6 m/s",
          "44.6 m/s"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "The initial velocity is −25 m/s downward, so $v$ = −(25) − (9.8)(2) = −44.6 m/s.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_kin_4",
        "topic": "Kinematics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "A rocket is propelled upward with an acceleration of 25 m/$s^{2}$ for 5 s. After that time, the engine is shut off, and the rocket continues to move upward. The maximum height, in meters, that the rocket will reach is</p>",
        "options": [
          "900",
          "1,000",
          "1,100",
          "1,200"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "The rocket accelerates from rest, so the first distance traveled in 5 s is given by</p> v_x = v_0\\cos(30^\\circ) = 40(0.866) = 34.6\\text{ m/s} $$\r\n<p class=\"expt\">Substituting the values for time (5 s) and acceleration (25 m/$s^{2}$) gives $y_{1}$ = 312.5 m. After 5 s of accelerating, the rocket has a velocity of 125 m/s. After this time, the engine stops and the rocket is decelerated by gravity as it continues to move upward. The time to decelerate to zero is found by dividing 125 m/s by the acceleration of gravity. Thus, 125/9.8 = 12.76 s.</p>\r\n<p class=\"expt\">The distance traveled during that time is added to the first accelerated distance. The second distance is given by</p> v = \\sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = \\sqrt{(34.6)^2 + (10.2)^2} = 36.1\\text{ m/s} $$\r\n<p class=\"expt\">The total distance traveled is therefore equal to 1,108 m or, rounded off, 1,100 m.</p></li>\r\n<li>"

        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "An object has an initial velocity of 15 m/s. How long must it accelerate at a constant rate of 3 m/$s^{2}$ before its average velocity is equal to twice its initial velocity?</p>",

          "10 s",
          "15 s",

        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "In the situation shown below, what is the tension in string 1?</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\"><img alt=\"\" class=\"w51\" role=\"presentation\" src=\"images/f082-01.jpg\"/></p>",
        "options": [
          "69.3 N",
          "98 N",
          "138.6 N",
          "147.6 N"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "We need to apply the second law for static equilibrium. This means that we must resolve the tensions into their $x$- and $y$-components. The $y$-component of $T_{1}$ must balance the weight = <i>mg</i> = 49 N. Thus, $T_{1}$ sin 45 = 49 N and $T_{1}$ = 69.3 N.</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\"><img alt=\"\" class=\"w28\" role=\"presentation\" src=\"images/f085-01.jpg\"/></p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_dyn_2",
        "topic": "Newton's Laws & Forces",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Two masses, $M$ and $m$, are hung over a massless, frictionless pulley as shown below. If $M$ &gt; $m$, what is the downward acceleration of mass $M$?</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\"><img alt=\"\" class=\"w51\" role=\"presentation\" src=\"images/f082-02.jpg\"/></p>",
        "options": [
          "$g$",
          "$ \\mu_s = 0.5 $",
          "$ \\mu_s > 0.5 $",
          "$ \\mu_s < 0.5 $"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "The free-body diagrams for both masses, $M$ and $m$, look like this:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\"><img alt=\"\" class=\"w43\" role=\"presentation\" src=\"images/f085-02.jpg\"/></p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">The large mass is accelerating downward, while the small mass is accelerating upward. The tension in the string is directed upward, while gravity, given by the weight, is directed downward. Using the second law for accelerated motion, we must show that for each mass, ∑$F$<sub>$y$</sub> = <i>ma</i>. Thus, we have</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$T - Mg = -Ma \\text{ and } T - mg = ma$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Eliminating the tension $T$ and solving for $a$ gives us ($M$ − $m$)$g$/($M +m$).</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },

        "topic": "Newton's Laws & Forces",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "A 0.25-kg mass is attached to a string and swung in a vertical circle whose radius is 0.75 m. At the bottom of the circle, the mass is observed to have a speed of 10 m/s. What is the magnitude of the tension in the string at that point?</p>",
        "options": [
          "2.45 N",
          "5.78 N",
          "22.6 N",
          "35.7 N"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "A sketch of the situation is shown below:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$\\text{[Diagram of vertical circle: radius } r = 0.5\\text{ m}, \\text{mass } m, \\text{tension } \\vec{T}, \\text{gravity } m\\vec{g}]$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">At the lowest point, the downward force of gravity is opposed by the upward tension in the string. Note that doing a quick tip-to-tail graphical solution of the force vectors must result in an upward (inward) net force. Thus, we can write</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$T - mg = \\frac{mv^2}{r}$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Substituting in the given values and solving for $T$ gives us 35.7 N.</p></li>\r\n<li>"

Using our circular motion convention of inward forces being positive, we can write</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$mg - N = \\frac{mv^2}{r}$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">A sketch is shown below. Note that doing a quick tip-to-tail graphical solution of the force vectors must result in a downward (inward) net force. Substituting in the given values and solving for $N$ gives 7,300 N upward.</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\"><img alt=\"\" class=\"w53\" role=\"presentation\" src=\"images/f085-07.jpg\"/></p></li>\r\n<li>"

        "options": [
          "3 m",
          "87 m",
          "48 m",
          "58 m"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "With horizontal motion, the normal force is equal to the force of gravity. When the puck is moving with constant velocity, no net force is acting on it. Thus, when friction acts to slow the puck down, the friction is the only net force. Therefore, we write</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$f = \\mu N = \\mu mg = -ma$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">(since the puck is decelerating). Substituting the known numbers gives a deceleration of −3.43 m/$s^{2}$. Now, the final velocity will be zero; and since the time to stop is unknown, we use the following kinematic expression to solve for the stopping distance:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$-v_i^2 = 2ax$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Substituting the known numbers, we obtain approximately 58 m as the distance the puck will travel before stopping.</p></li>\r\n<li>"

        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "A force of 20 N acts horizontally on a mass of 10 kg being pushed along a frictionless incline that makes a 30° angle with the horizontal, as shown below.</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\"><img alt=\"\" class=\"w48\" role=\"presentation\" src=\"images/f083-02.jpg\"/></p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">The magnitude of the acceleration of the mass up the incline is equal to</p>",

  "ap-topic-phys1-energy": {
    "id": "ap-topic-phys1-energy",
    "title": "AP Physics 1: Work, Energy & Power",
    "subtitle": "Work-energy theorem, kinetic and potential energy, conservation of mechanical energy, power",
    "timeLimitMinutes": 20,
    "testType": "Topic Test",
    "subject": "AP Physics 1",
    "topic": "Energy & Work",
    "questions": [
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_ene_1",
        "topic": "Energy & Work",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Which of the following are the units for the spring constant, <span>$k$</span>?</p>",
        "options": [
          "kg · $m^{2}$/$s^{2}$",
          "kg · $s^{2}$",
          "kg · m/s",
          "kg/$s^{2}$"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "The units for the spring or force constant are provided by Hooke’s law, $F$ = <i>kx</i>, and are newtons per meter. Recall that 1 N = 1 kg m/$s^{2}$, so dividing by $m$ gives kg/$s^{2}$.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_ene_2",
        "topic": "Energy & Work",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Which of the following is an expression for mechanical power?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<i>Ft</i>/$m$",
          "$F$ <sup>2</sup>$m$/$a$",
          "<i>Fm</i><sup>2</sup>/$t$",
          "$F$ <sup>2</sup>$t$/$m$"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Power is equal to work done divided by time. Therefore,</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$P = \\frac{W}{t} = \\frac{Fd}{t}$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Using some algebra and kinematics, we see that</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$P = \\frac{Fd}{t} = Fv = Fat = F\\left(\\frac{F}{m}\\right)t = \\frac{F^2 t}{m}$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">You could also get the answer by verifying which expression has units of joules per second.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_ene_3",
        "topic": "Energy & Work",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "A pendulum consisting of a mass $m$ attached to a light string of length <i>ℓ</i> is displaced from its rest position, making an angle θ with the vertical. It is then released and allowed to swing freely. Which of the following expressions represents the velocity of the mass when it reaches its lowest position?</p>",
        "options": [
          "$ 0.5\\text{ J} $",
          "$ 1.0\\text{ J} $",
          "$ 2.0\\text{ J} $",
          "$ 4.0\\text{ J} $"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "Consider the sketch below of the situation:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\"><img alt=\"\" class=\"w55\" role=\"presentation\" src=\"images/f104-03.jpg\"/></p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">From the geometry of the sketch, note that</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$h = \\ell - \\ell\\cos\\theta = \\ell(1 - \\cos\\theta)$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">If it is assumed that there is no friction, gravity is the only conservative force acting to do work. Therefore,</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$ME_{\\text{bottom}} = ME_{\\text{top}}, KE_{\\text{bottom}} = PE_{\\text{top}}, \\frac{1}{2}m v^2 = mgh$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">and so, at the bottom,</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$v = \\sqrt{2gh} = \\sqrt{2g\\ell(1 - \\cos\\theta)}$</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_ene_4",
        "topic": "Energy & Work",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "An engine maintains constant power on a conveyor belt machine. If the belt’s velocity is doubled, the magnitude of its average acceleration</p>",
        "options": [
          "is doubled",
          "is quartered",
          "is halved",
          "is quadrupled"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "Power is equal to the product of the average force applied times the velocity. If the velocity is doubled, and the power is constant, the average force must be halved. Since $F$ = <i>ma</i>, the average acceleration of the belt must be halved as well.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_ene_5",
        "topic": "Energy & Work",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "A mass $m$ is moving horizontally along a nearly frictionless floor with velocity $v$. The mass now encounters a part of the floor that has a coefficient of kinetic friction given by $\\mu$. The total distance traveled by the mass before it is slowed by friction to a stop is given by</p>",
        "options": [
          "2$v^{2}$/<i>μg</i>",
          "$v^{2}$/2<i>μg</i>",
          "2<i>μgv</i><sup>2</sup>",
          "<i>μv</i><sup>2</sup>/2$g$"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "The only applied force is friction, which is doing work to stop the mass. This work is being taken from the initial kinetic energy. For friction, we know that $f$ = <i>μN</i>, and since the motion is horizontal, $N$ = <i>mg</i>. Let $x$ be the distance traveled while stopping; therefore, we can write that $W$<sub>$f$</sub> = <i>KE</i> and:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\"><img alt=\"\" class=\"w21\" role=\"presentation\" src=\"images/f104-05a.jpg\"/></p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Solving for $x$, we get:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$x = \\frac{v^2}{2\\mu g}$</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_ene_6",
        "topic": "Energy & Work",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "Two unequal masses are dropped simultaneously from the same height. The two masses will experience the same change in</p>",
        "options": [
          "acceleration",
          "kinetic energy",
          "potential energy",
          "velocity"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Objects dropped simultaneously from the same height have the same constant acceleration, which is the change in velocity. The unequal masses will provide for different energies, but the velocity changes will be the same.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_ene_7",
        "topic": "Energy & Work",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "A pendulum that consists of a 2-kg mass swings to a maximum vertical displacement of 17 cm above its rest position. At its lowest point, the kinetic energy of the mass is equal to</p>",
        "options": [
          "0.33 J",
          "3.33 J",
          "33.3 J",
          "333 J"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "Since we have a conservative system,</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$KE_{\\text{bottom}} = PE_{\\text{top}} = mgh = (2)(9.8)(0.17)$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Remember to change 17 cm to 0.17 m!</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_ene_8",
        "topic": "Energy & Work",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "A 0.3-kg mass rests on top of a spring that has been compressed by 0.04 m. Neglect any frictional effects, and consider the spring to be massless. Then, if the spring has a constant $k$ equal to 2,000 N/m, to what height will the mass rise when the system is released?</p>",
        "options": [
          "1.24 m",
          "0.75 m",
          "0.54 m",
          "1.04 m"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "We are dealing with a conservative system, so the initial starting energy is just the potential energy of the compressed spring. This energy supplies the work needed to raise the mass a height $h$, which is a gain in gravitational potential energy. Thus, we equate these two expressions and solve for the height:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$\\frac{1}{2}(2,000)(0.4)^2 = (0.3)(9.8)h$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Thus, $h$ = 0.54 m.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },

        "difficulty": "hard",

        "topic": "Gravitation",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "What is the value of $g$ at a height above Earth’s surface that is equal to the radius of Earth?</p>",
        "options": [
          "9.8 N/kg",
          "4.9 N/kg",
          "6.93 N/kg",
          "2.45 N/kg"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "The value of $g$ varies inversely with the square of the distance from the center of Earth; therefore, if we double the distance from the center (as in this case), the value of $g$ decreases by one-fourth: 1/4(9.8) = 2.45. Since $g = F$/$m$, alternative units are newtons per kilogram.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_grav_2",
        "topic": "Gravitation",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "A planet has half the mass of Earth and half the radius. Compared to the acceleration due to gravity near the surface of Earth, the acceleration of gravity near the surface of this other planet is</p>",
        "options": [
          "twice as much",
          "one-fourth as much",
          "half as much",
          "the same"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "If, using the formula for $g$, we take half the mass, the value decreases by one-half. If we decrease the radius by half, the value will increase by four times. Combining both effects results in an overall increase of two times.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_grav_3",
        "topic": "Gravitation",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Which of the following is an expression for the acceleration of gravity at the surface of a planet with uniform density ρ and radius <span>$r$</span>?</p>",
        "options": [
          "$G$(4πρ/3$r^{2}$)",
          "$G$(4πρ$r^{2}$/3)",
          "$G$(4πρ/3$r$)",
          "$G$(4π$r$ρ/3)"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "The formula for $g$ is $g$ = <i>GM</i>/$r^{2}$. The planet is essentially a sphere of mass $M$, radius $r$, and density ρ (with $M = V$ρ, where $V$ is the volume). The volume of the planet is given by $V$ = 4/3<i>πr</i><sup>3</sup>. Making the substitutions yields:</p> g = \\frac{GM}{r^2} \\implies g' = \\frac{GM}{(2R)^2} = \\frac{g}{4} = \\frac{9.8}{4} = 2.45\\text{ N/kg} $$</li>\r\n<li>"
      },

        "id": "tp_phys1_grav_4",
        "topic": "Gravitation",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "What is the orbital velocity of a satellite at a height of 300 km above the surface of Earth? (The mass of Earth is approximately 6 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg, and its radius is 6.4 × 10<span><sup>6</sup></span> m.)</p>",
        "options": [
          "5.42 × 10<sup>1</sup> m/s",
          "1.15 × 10<sup>6</sup> m/s",
          "7.7 × 10<sup>3</sup> m/s",
          "6 × 10<sup>6</sup> m/s"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "The formula for orbital velocity is</p> v_{\\text{orbit}} = \\sqrt{\\frac{GM}{r}} $$\r\n<p class=\"nump\">where $r$ is the distance from the center of Earth. In this case, we must add 300 km = 300,000 m to the radius of Earth. Thus, $r$ = 6.7 × 10<sup>6</sup> m.       },

        "topic": "Gravitation",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "What is the escape velocity from the Moon, given that the mass of the Moon is 7.2 × 10<sup>22</sup> kg and its radius is 1.778 <span>×</span> 10<span><sup>6</sup></span> m?</p>",
        "options": [
          "1.64 × 10<sup>3</sup> m/s",
          "2.32 × 10<sup>3</sup> m/s",

        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "The formula for escape velocity is</p> T = 2\\pi\\sqrt{\\frac{r^3}{GM}} $$\r\n<p class=\"nump\">Substituting the given values yields $v_{esc}$ = 2,324 or 2.32 × 10<sup>3</sup> m/s.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },

        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "A black hole theoretically has an escape velocity that is greater than or equal to the velocity of light (3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s).   "ap-topic-phys1-rotation": {
    "id": "ap-topic-phys1-rotation",
    "title": "AP Physics 1: Rotational Motion & Torque",
    "subtitle": "Torque, static equilibrium, rotational inertia, rotational kinematics, rolling objects, angular momentum",
    "timeLimitMinutes": 25,
    "testType": "Topic Test",
    "subject": "AP Physics 1",
    "topic": "Rotational Motion",
    "questions": [
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_rot_1",
        "topic": "Rotational Motion",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "<p>A 45-kg girl is sitting on a seesaw 0.6 m to the left of the central fulcrum. How far to the right of the fulcrum should a 60-kg boy sit so that the seesaw balances horizontally in rotational equilibrium?</p>",
        "options": [
          "0.30 m",
          "0.35 m",
          "0.40 m",
          "0.45 m"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "To remain in balance, the two torques must be equal. The force on each side is given by the weight, <i>mg</i>. The moment arm distances are 0.6 m and $x$. Since the factor $g$ will appear on both sides of the torque balance equation, we can eliminate it and write</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$(45)(0.6) = (60)x \\text{ implies } x = 0.45\\text{ m}$</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_rot_2",
        "topic": "Rotational Motion",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "<p>A uniform meter stick is pivoted at the 50-cm mark. A 20-g mass is suspended at the 20-cm mark (30 cm from the fulcrum), and a 15-g mass is suspended at the 70-cm mark (20 cm from the fulcrum). What is the position on the meter stick where a 10-g mass should be hung to balance the stick horizontally?</p>",
        "options": [
          "80 cm mark",
          "60 cm mark",
          "75 cm mark",
          "25 cm mark",
          "90 cm mark"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "Torque equilibrium about the 50-cm pivot: Counter-clockwise torque = (20 g)(30 cm) = 600 g·cm. Clockwise torque from 15 g mass = (15 g)(20 cm) = 300 g·cm. Deficit on clockwise side = 600 - 300 = 300 g·cm. The 10-g mass must be placed at distance d to the right: (10 g)(d) = 300 => d = 30 cm to the right of the 50-cm mark, which is at the 80 cm mark."
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_rot_3",
        "topic": "Rotational Motion",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "<p>A solid stepped cylinder consists of an outer radius r_1 = 0.4 m and an inner hub radius r_2 = 0.2 m, pivoted on a frictionless axle. A string wound around the outer cylinder pulls with force F_1 = 30 N clockwise, and a string wound around the inner hub pulls with force F_2 = 50 N counter-clockwise. What is the net torque on the cylinder?</p>",
        "options": [
          "2.25 N · m",
          "−2.25 N · m",
          "0.5 N · m",
          "−0.5 N · m"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "The net torque is given by the vector sum of all torques. \\vec{F}<sub>2</sub> provides a counterclockwise positive torque, while \\vec{F}<sub>1</sub> provides a clockwise negative torque. Each radius is the necessary moment arm distance. Thus, we have</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$\\tau_{\\text{net}} = (5)(0.35) - (3)(0.75) = -0.5\\text{ N}\\cdot\\text{m}$</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_rot_4",
        "topic": "Rotational Motion",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "What is the net torque about an axis through point <span>$A$</span>?</p>",
        "options": [
          "16.8 N · m",
          "15.2 N · m",
          "−5.5 N · m",
          "−7.8 N · m"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "In this problem, the net torque about point $A$ implies that the force passing through point $A$ does not contribute to the net torque. Also, we need the components of the remaining forces perpendicular to the beam. From the diagram, we see that the 30-N force acts counterclockwise (positive), while the 10-N force acts clockwise (negative). Thus:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$\\tau_{\\text{net}} = (30)(\\cos 45^\\circ)(1.5) - (10)(\\sin 30^\\circ)(3) = 16.8\\text{ N}\\cdot\\text{m}$</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_rot_5",
        "topic": "Rotational Motion",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "What is the net torque about an axis through point <span>$C$</span>?</p>",
        "options": [
          "3.5 N · m",
          "7.5 N · m",
          "−15.2 N · m",
          "5.9 N · m"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "In this problem, since the pivot is now set at point $C$, we can eliminate the 30-N force passing through point $C$ as a contributor to the torque. Again, we see that the 20-N force will act in a counterclockwise direction, while the 10-N force will act clockwise. Each force is 1.5 m from the pivot. We also need the component of each force perpendicular to the beam. Thus:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$\\tau_{\\text{net}} = (20)(\\sin 30^\\circ)(1.5) - (10)(\\sin 30^\\circ)(1.5) = 7.5\\text{ N}\\cdot\\text{m}$</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_rot_6",
        "topic": "Rotational Motion",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "Compute the average angular acceleration and the angular displacement during the 2 seconds a rotating object speeds up from 0.5 rad/s to 0.7 rad/s.</p>",
        "options": [
          "α = 0.1 rad/$s^{2}$    Δθ = 0.3 radians",
          "α = 0.2 rad/$s^{2}$    Δθ = 0.5 radians",
          "α = 0.1 rad/$s^{2}$    Δθ = 1.2 radians",
          "α = 0.2 rad/$s^{2}$    Δθ = 1.2 radians"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "$ \\tau_{\\text{net}} = I\\alpha $</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$\\Delta\\theta = \\omega_0 t + \\frac{1}{2}\\alpha t^2 = 0.5(2) + \\frac{1}{2}(0.1)(2)^2 = 1 + 0.2 = 1.2\\text{ radians}$</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_rot_7",
        "topic": "Rotational Motion",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "An object with a rotational inertia $I$ experiences a net torque of $T$. If the object is initially at rest, what is its angular speed after 3 seconds of this torque?</p>",
        "options": [
          "3<i>I T</i>",
          "9<i>I T</i>",

          "3$T$/$I$"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Since τ = $I$α and $ L = I\\omega $ we can combine and solve for Δω:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$\\Delta\\omega = (T/I)\\Delta t = 3T/I$</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {

        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "If a spinning ball of clay on top of a freely turning frictionless tabletop increases its rotational inertia by 50 percent by bulging outward, what will happen to the rotational speed of the clay and tabletop?</p>",

        "topic": "Oscillatory Motion",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "What is the length of a pendulum whose period, at the equator, is 1 s?</p>",
        "options": [
          "0.15 m",
          "0.25 m",
          "0.30 m",
          "0.45 m"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "If we use the formula for the period of a pendulum, $ T = 2\\pi\\sqrt{\\frac{L}{g}} $, and square both sides, we can solve for the length:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$\\ell = T^2 \\frac{g}{4\\pi^2}$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Using the values given in the question, we find that <i>ℓ</i> = 0.25 m.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_shm_2",
        "topic": "Oscillatory Motion",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "On a planet, an astronaut determines the acceleration of gravity by means of a pendulum. She observes that the 1-m-long pendulum has a period of 1.5 s. The acceleration of gravity, in meters per second squared, on the planet is</p>",
        "options": [
          "7.5",
          "15.2",
          "10.2",
          "17.5"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Again using the formula for the period of a pendulum, this time we solve for the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity:</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$g = 4\\frac{\\pi\\ell}{T^2}$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Using the values given in the question, we find that $g$ = 17.5 m/$s^{2}$.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_shm_3",
        "topic": "Oscillatory Motion",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "When a 0.05-kg mass is attached to a vertical spring, it is observed that the spring stretches 0.03 m. The system is then placed horizontally on a frictionless surface and set into simple harmonic motion. What is the period of the oscillations?</p>",
        "options": [
          "0.75 s",
          "0.12 s",
          "0.35 s",
          "1.3 s"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "We first find the spring constant. From $F$ = <i>kx</i>, we see that</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$F = mg = (0.05)(9.8) = 0.49\\text{ N}$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Thus,</p>\r\n<p class=\"center1\">$k = \\frac{F}{x} = \\frac{0.49}{0.03} = 16.3\\text{ N/m}$</p>\r\n<p class=\"exp\">Now the period is given by the formula $T =  T = 2\\pi\\sqrt{\\frac{m}{k}} $. Using the values given in the question, we find that $T$ = 0.35 s.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {

        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "A mass of 0.5 kg is connected to a massless spring with a force constant $k$ of 50 N/m. The system is oscillating on a frictionless, horizontal surface. If the amplitude of the oscillations is 2 cm, the total energy of the system is</p>",
        "options": [
          "0.01 J",
          "0.1 J",
          "0.5 J",
          "0.3 J"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "The formula for total energy is $E$ = (1/2)<i>kA</i><sup>2</sup>. Using the values given in the question, we get $E$ = 0.01 J.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_shm_5",
        "topic": "Oscillatory Motion",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "A mass of 0.3 kg is connected to a massless spring with a force constant $k$ of 20 N/m. The system oscillates horizontally on a frictionless surface with an amplitude of 4 cm. What is the velocity of the mass when it is 2 cm from its equilibrium position?</p>",
        "options": [

  "ap-topic-phys1-fluids": {
    "id": "ap-topic-phys1-fluids",
    "title": "AP Physics 1: Fluids & Bernoulli's Principle",
    "subtitle": "Fluid statics, Pascal's principle, buoyant force, Archimedes principle, fluid dynamics and Bernoulli's equation",

    "testType": "Topic Test",

    "topic": "Fluids",
    "questions": [
      {

        "topic": "Fluids",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "The rate of flow of a liquid from a hole in a container depends on all of the following except</p>",
        "options": [
          "the density of the liquid",
          "the height of the liquid above the hole",
          "the area of the hole",
          "the acceleration of gravity"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "The flow rate of a liquid from a hole does not depend on the density of the liquid.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_flu_2",
        "topic": "Fluids",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "A person is standing on a railroad station platform when a high-speed train passes by. The person will tend to be</p>",
        "options": [
          "pushed away from the train",
          "pulled in toward the train",
          "pushed upward into the air",
          "pulled down into the ground"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "Because of the Bernoulli effect, the speeding train reduces the air pressure between the person and the train. This pressure difference creates a force tending to pull the person into the train. Be very careful when standing on a train platform!</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {
        "id": "tp_phys1_flu_3",
        "topic": "Fluids",
        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Bernoulli’s equation is based on which law of physics?</p>",
        "options": [
          "Conservation of linear momentum",
          "Conservation of angular momentum",
          "Newton’s first law of motion",
          "Conservation of energy"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Bernoulli’s principle was developed as an application of conservation of energy.</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },

        "difficulty": "medium",

        "options": [

          "(rate of flow)/(pressure)",
          "(pressure) × (velocity)/(area)"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "Power is expressed in J/s. The product of pressure (force divided by area) and flow rate ($m^{3}$/s) leads to newtons times meters over seconds (J/s).</p></li>\r\n<li>"
      },
      {

        "topic": "Fluids",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "Which of the following statements is an expression of the equation of continuity?</p>",

          "Pressure in a static fluid is transmitted uniformly throughout.",
          "Fluid flows faster through a narrower pipe."
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "The equation of continuity states that the product of velocity and area is a constant for a given fluid. A consequence of this is that a fluid moves faster through a narrower pipe.</p></li>\r\n<li>"

          "1,200 W",

        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "Two objects are thrown vertically upward from the same initial height. One object has twice the initial velocity of the other. Neglecting any air resistance, the object with the greater initial velocity will rise to a maximum height that is</p>",
        "options": [
          "twice that of the other object, assuming they have the same mass",
          "twice that of the other object, independent of their masses",
          "four times that of the other object, assuming they have the same mass",
          "four times that of the other object, independent of their masses"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "Twice the initial vertical velocity will give twice the time in flight. Average vertical velocity will also be doubled.       },

        "difficulty": "easy",
        "question": "A 2-kilogram cart has a velocity of 4 meters per second to the right. It collides with a 5-kilogram cart moving to the left at 1 meter per second. After the collision, the two carts stick together. Can the magnitude and the direction of the velocity of the two carts after the collision be determined from the given information?</p>",
        "options": [
          "No, since the collision is inelastic, we must know the energy lost.",

        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "Conservation of momentum:</p> m_1 v_{1i} + m_2 v_{2i} = (m_1 + m_2) v_f \\implies (2)(4) + (5)(-1) = 7 v_f \\implies v_f = \\frac{3}{7}\\text{ m/s (to the right)} $$\r\n<p class=\"numpt\">The collision is inelastic since the carts stick together.</p></li>\r\n<li>"

        "explanation": "(B) This is a question about electrostatic induction. Because this charge redistribution results in moving negative charge closer to the positive point charge and moving positive charge farther away from the positive point charge, it increases the attractive force between the metal sphere and the positive point charge. Therefore, compared to an insulating sphere with the same net charge, a metal sphere always experiences a greater attractive force (such that charged metal > charged insulator and uncharged metal > uncharged insulator).         "question": "<p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/t0301-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindentt\"><strong>Time:</strong> 45 minutes. You may refer to the constants sheet and the equation sheet, both of which are found in the appendix. You may use a calculator.</p><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_1\" id=\"ch19p_1\">1.</a></strong> An object moves along the positive $x$-axis. The net force on the object as a function of time $t$ measured in seconds is given in newtons by the function $F$($t$) = 3$t^{2} +t$ + 2. What is the impulse delivered to the object during the first second of motion?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>4.0 N⋅s</p>",
          "<p>3.5 N⋅s</p>",
          "<p>0 N⋅s</p>",
          "<p>7.0 N⋅s</p>",
          "<p>6.0 N⋅s</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_1\" id=\"rch19p_1\">1.</a></strong> <strong>B</strong>—Impulse is the integral of force with respect to time. That’s $t^{3} +t^{2}$/2 + 2$t$, evaluated from 0 to 1 second: 1 + ½ + 2 = 3.5 N⋅s.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_2",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_2\" id=\"ch19p_2\">2.</a></strong> A cart moves along a straight track. Its position $x$ as a function of time is given in meters by the equation $x$ = 2$t^{3} +t^{2}$ – 2$t$. What is the cart’s acceleration at time $t$ = 4 s?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>102 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>10 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>133 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>12 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>50 m/$s^{2}$</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "E",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_2\" id=\"rch19p_2\">2.</a></strong> <strong>E—</strong>Acceleration is the second time derivative of position. The second derivative of the given function is $a$ = 12$t$ + 2. Plug in $t$ = 4 s to get an acceleration of 50 m/$s^{2}$.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_3",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0303-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_3\" id=\"ch19p_3\">3.</a></strong> An object of mass $m$ is attached to a vertical spring, as shown above. When the string is unstretched, it is of length $L$. When the object is gently attached and allowed to hang from rest, the string is of length $L +x$. Now the object is attached, released from rest while the spring is at its unstretched length $L$, and allowed to oscillate. What is the maximum length of the spring during the oscillations?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>$L$ + <img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/s2x.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p>2$L$ + 2$x$</p>",
          "<p>2$L$ + <img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/s2x.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p>$L$ + 2$x$</p>",
          "<p>$L$ + 4$x$</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_3\" id=\"rch19p_3\">3.</a></strong> <strong>D</strong>—The equilibrium position is the midpoint of any oscillations. So $L +x$ is the equilibrium position. The object was released a distance $x$ above the equilibrium position, meaning $x$ is the amplitude of the oscillations. The spring will reach a distance $x$ both above and below the equilibrium, meaning the spring will oscillate between a length $L$ and ($L +x$) $+x$. That’s $L$ + 2$x$ as the maximum length.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_4",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0303-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 4 and 5: Two carts move along a smooth surface as shown above. Cart A of mass 3.1 kg moves west with speed 1.2 m/s. Cart B of mass 1.3 kg moves north with speed 2.2 m/s. The carts collide and stick together, moving at angle $\\theta$ above west.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_4\" id=\"ch19p_4\">4.</a></strong> What is the speed of the center of mass of the two-cart system before collision?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>2.5 m/s</p>",
          "<p>3.4 m/s</p>",
          "<p>1.1 m/s</p>",
          "<p>1.6 m/s</p>",
          "<p>2.3 m/s</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_4\" id=\"rch19p_4\">4.</a></strong> <strong>C—</strong>Use conservation of momentum to find the total momentum before collision. Momentum is mass times velocity. For cart A before collision that’s 3.72 N⋅s west; for cart B before collision that’s 2.86 N⋅s north. The total momentum before collision is the Pythagorean sum of these—because momentum is a vector, direction matters. So total momentum before collision is 4.69 N⋅s at the angle $\\theta$. Conservation of momentum means that this is also the total momentum after collision. Since the carts stick together, just divide this by the 4.4 kg mass to get the speed after collision of 1.07 m/s. And since no external forces act on the two-cart system, its center of mass always moves at this speed. So answer is closest to C.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_5",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0303-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 4 and 5: Two carts move along a smooth surface as shown above. Cart A of mass 3.1 kg moves west with speed 1.2 m/s. Cart B of mass 1.3 kg moves north with speed 2.2 m/s. The carts collide and stick together, moving at angle $\\theta$ above west.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_5\" id=\"ch19p_5\">5.</a></strong> Which of the following methods will calculate the angle $\\theta$?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>Divide cart B’s speed by cart A’s speed, and take the inverse tangent of the result.</p>",
          "<p>Calculate the momentum of each cart by multiplying mass times speed. Then divide cart B’s momentum by cart A’s momentum, and take the inverse tangent of the result.</p>",
          "<p>Calculate the kinetic energy of each cart by multiplying ½ by its mass times its speed squared. Then divide the cart B’s kinetic energy by cart A’s kinetic energy, and take the inverse tangent of the result.</p>",
          "<p>Divide the square of cart B’s speed by the square of cart A’s speed, and take the inverse tangent of the result.</p>",
          "<p>Divide cart B’s mass by cart A’s mass, and take the inverse tangent of the result.</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_5\" id=\"rch19p_5\">5.</a></strong> <strong>B—</strong>Momentum is a vector and is conserved separately in each direction in a collision. The total momentum on the vertical axis is just cart B’s momentum, and on the horizontal axis, just cart A’s momentum. The inverse tangent of these momentum components gives the direction of the total momentum vector. And the direction of a velocity—of movement—is always the same as the direction of momentum. (You can’t just use the inverse tangent on the velocity components, because velocity isn’t conserved in a collision!)</p>"
      },

        "question": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_6\" id=\"ch19p_6\">6.</a></strong> A pendulum and a spring both oscillate in harmonic motion with small amplitude.           "Graph B: Pendulum T decreases inversely with m; Spring T increases linearly with m",

          "Graph D: Pendulum T increases as m^2; Spring T is horizontal",

        "answer": "C",

The period of an object on a spring is <img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0330-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/>, which depends on the square root of $m$, as in <strong>C</strong>.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_7",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_7\" id=\"ch19p_7\">7.</a></strong> Cart A is initially moving to the right toward stationary cart B. The carts collide and bounce off one another. Which of the following is correct about whether the horizontal linear momentum and the kinetic energy of the two-cart system are conserved in the collision?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>Linear momentum must be conserved. Kinetic energy may possibly be conserved.</p>",
          "<p>Linear momentum may possibly be conserved. Kinetic energy must be conserved.</p>",
          "<p>Linear momentum may possibly be conserved. Kinetic energy may possibly be conserved.</p>",
          "<p>Linear momentum must be conserved. Kinetic energy must be conserved.</p>",
          "<p>Linear momentum must be conserved. Kinetic energy must not be conserved.</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_7\" id=\"rch19p_7\">7.</a></strong> <strong>A—</strong>Linear momentum is conserved in any collision because there are no external forces acting on the two-cart system. By definition, elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy. It’s true that for a collision to be elastic, the carts must bounce, but just because carts bounce doesn’t mean the collision <em>must</em> be elastic.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_8",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_8\" id=\"ch19p_8\">8.</a></strong> A block slides down a frictionless ramp on Earth’s surface. The ramp makes an angle $\\theta$ above the horizontal, and the block’s acceleration down the incline is $a$. Now, the block slides down the same ramp near a different planet’s surface. The ramp still makes an angle $\\theta$ above the horizontal. This different planet has twice the density of Earth but the same radius. What is the acceleration of the block sliding down the ramp on the different planet?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>(1/2)$a$</p>",
          "<p>2$a$</p>",
          "<p>$a$</p>",
          "<p>(1/4)$a$</p>",
          "<p>4$a$</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_8\" id=\"rch19p_8\">8.</a></strong> <strong>B</strong>—The unbalanced force down the incline is <em>mg</em> sin $\\theta$. Newton’s second law shows that the acceleration is then $g$ sin $\\theta$. So however $g$ changes, that’s how the acceleration changes. The formula for the gravitational field near a planet is $g$ = <em>GM</em>/$r^{2}$. But we’re given density, not mass! Density is mass per volume. So multiply numerator and denominator by $r$ to get $g$ = <em>GMr</em>/$r^{3}$. Now <em>M/r</em><sup>3</sup> is density . . . so $g$ = <em>G(density)r</em>. The universal gravitation constant $G$ can’t change, the problem says the radius $r$ doesn’t change, but the density doubles—so the whole term for $g$ doubles. And so does the acceleration.</p>"
      },

        "options": [

          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/darrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/1arrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/uarrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",

        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_9\" id=\"rch19p_9\">9.</a></strong> <strong>B—</strong>The instantaneous velocity is in the direction the object is moving at this instant. That’s straight down the page.</p>"
      },

        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",

        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0305-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 9–11: A particle moves clockwise in a horizontal circle of radius 2.0 m, as shown above. At the moment in which the particle is at the position shown, its speed is 3.0 m/s, and its speed is increasing by 2.5 m/s per second.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_10\" id=\"ch19p_10\">10.</a></strong> Which of the following vectors could represent the direction of the net force on the particle at the position shown?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/larrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/darrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/1arrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/uarrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/2arrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>"
        ],
        "answer": "E",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_10\" id=\"rch19p_10\">10.</a></strong> <strong>E—</strong>The net force is in the direction of acceleration. The acceleration has two components here: one toward the center (the “centripetal” acceleration) and another in the direction of motion because the particle is speeding up (the “tangential” acceleration). So the acceleration, and the net force, points somewhat left toward the center and somewhat down.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_11",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0305-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 9–11: A particle moves clockwise in a horizontal circle of radius 2.0 m, as shown above. At the moment in which the particle is at the position shown, its speed is 3.0 m/s, and its speed is increasing by 2.5 m/s per second.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_11\" id=\"ch19p_11\">11.</a></strong> What is the magnitude of the particle’s instantaneous acceleration at the position shown?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>3.6 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>1.5 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>4.5 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>5.1 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>2.5 m/$s^{2}$</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_11\" id=\"rch19p_11\">11.</a></strong> <strong>D—</strong>The acceleration has two components, which must be added using the Pythagorean theorem. The centripetal component is $v^{2}$/$r$, which is (3 m/s)<sup>2</sup>/(2 m) = 4.5 m/$s^{2}$. The tangential component is given as 2.5 m/$s^{2}$. So add 4.5<sup>2</sup> + 2.5<sup>2</sup> and take the square root to get 5.1 m/$s^{2}$.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_12",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
