        "question": "<p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0305-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_12\" id=\"ch19p_12\">12.</a></strong> Two blocks move across a rough table at constant speed. Friction is NOT negligible on any surface. The bottom block is pulled to the right with force $F$. Which of the following could indicate the direction of the total force of the bottom block on the top block?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/rarrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/larrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/1arrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/uarrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/3arrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_12\" id=\"rch19p_12\">12.</a></strong> <strong>D</strong>—The blocks move at constant speed and so experience balanced forces both vertically and horizontally. Vertically, the force of the bottom block on the top block has to balance the top block’s weight—and so has an upward component. Horizontally, the bottom block can’t exert a force on the top block, because there’s no other object to exert a balancing force. Thus no horizontal forces can act on the top block at all.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_13",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0306-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_13\" id=\"ch19p_13\">13.</a></strong> Three stones are thrown from a cliff with velocity vectors $v_{A}$, $v_{B}$, and $v_{C}$. The magnitude of the initial velocity for each stone is the same, but the directions of initial velocity are shown in the diagram. Which of the following correctly ranks the stones according to their speed upon hitting the level ground below the cliff, and by the magnitude of their vertical components of velocity upon hitting the ground?</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0306-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0306-03.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
        "options": [
          "Speed: v_A > v_B > v_C; Vertical Velocity: v_{yA} > v_{yB} > v_{yC}",
          "Speed: v_A > v_B > v_C; Vertical Velocity: v_{yA} = v_{yB} = v_{yC}",
          "Speed: v_A = v_B = v_C; Vertical Velocity: v_{yA} = v_{yB} = v_{yC}",
          "Speed: v_A < v_B < v_C; Vertical Velocity: v_{yA} < v_{yB} < v_{yC}",
          "Speed: v_A = v_B = v_C; Vertical Velocity: v_{yA} > v_{yB} > v_{yC}"
        ],
        "answer": "E",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_13\" id=\"rch19p_13\">13.</a></strong> <strong>E</strong>—For the magnitude of vertical velocity, start with the vertical component of initial velocity—A’s is largest, B’s is next largest, C’s is zero. Look at which goes highest: Kinematics equations simplify to $x = v^{2}$/2$a$ for final speed of zero, so the stone with the greatest initial vertical speed goes highest. Similarly, the one that goes highest hits the ground with greatest vertical speed. So the <em>vertical</em> velocity at ground is ranked A &gt; B &gt; C. As for speed at ground, it’s easiest to see this through energy conservation. All three rocks gain the same potential energy because they’re at the same vertical height from the ground. All three rocks start with the same initial kinetic energy because their speeds are the same. So the blocks must end up with the same kinetic energy as each other at the bottom, meaning also the same speed.</p>"
      },

        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 14–16: An object of mass $m$ is connected to a string of length $L$. The string is pulled back to an angle $θ_{1}$ and released from rest at position 1. Air resistance is NOT negligible. When the string is vertical, the object moves left. The object comes to rest again at position 3 when the string is at angle $θ_{3}$.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_14\" id=\"ch19p_14\">14.</a></strong> Which of the following is a correct expression for the work done by the air on the object between positions 1 and 2?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>½<em>mv</em><sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup></p>",
          "<p><em>mgL</em>$θ_{3}$</p>",
          "<p>½<em>mv</em><sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> - <em>mgL</em>$θ_{3}$</p>",
          "<p>½<em>mv</em><sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> - <em>mgL</em>$θ_{1}$</p>",
          "<p><em>mgL</em>$θ_{3}$ - <em>mgL</em>$θ_{1}$</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "E",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_14\" id=\"rch19p_14\">14.</a></strong> <strong>E—</strong>From position 1 to 2, the mechanical energy goes from all potential to all kinetic. Work is done by the air to reduce this mechanical energy. The reduction in mechanical energy is the difference between the kinetic energy at the bottom (½<em>mv</em><sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>) and the potential energy at the top (<em>mgLθ</em><sub>1</sub>).</p>"

        "options": [

          "<p>$θ_{3}$ is less than ½$θ_{1}$.</p>",
          "<p>The answer cannot be determined, but could be determined if we knew whether the force of air resistance were proportional to $v$ or $v^{2}$.</p>",
          "<p>The answer cannot be determined, even if we knew whether the force of air resistance were proportional to $v$ or $v^{2}$.</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "E",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_15\" id=\"rch19p_15\">15.</a></strong> <strong>E—</strong>If there’s a teeny bit of air resistance, then mechanical energy is almost conserved, and $θ_{3}$ is almost equal to $θ_{1}$. The object comes to rest again at position 3 when the string is at angle $θ_{3}$.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_16\" id=\"ch19p_16\">16.</a></strong> Now consider that the force of air resistance is equal to <em>cv</em>. Which of the following is a differential equation that could be used to solve for the angle $\\theta$ as a function of time while the string is between angles $θ_{1}$ and $θ_{2}$?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0307-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0307-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0307-03.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0307-04.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0307-05.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_16\" id=\"rch19p_16\">16.</a></strong> <strong>B—</strong>The forces in the direction of the object’s motion at any position have components <em>mg</em> sin $\\theta$ along the object’s path and <em>cv</em> against the object’s path. So the net force is <em>mg</em> sin $\\theta$ − <em>cv</em>. Set this equal to mass times acceleration, where acceleration is the second derivative of position. But we don’t want the derivative of the angle $\\theta$, we want the derivative of the distance along the arc. That’s <em>Lθ</em>.</p>"

      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_17",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 17–18: A cart moves along a straight road according to the velocity-time graph shown above.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_17\" id=\"ch19p_17\">17.</a></strong> What is the average acceleration of this car between time 0 and time 10 s?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>+0.3 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>0.0 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>+0.6 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>+1.0 m/$s^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>+3.0 m/$s^{2}$</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_17\" id=\"rch19p_17\">17.</a></strong> <strong>C—</strong>Acceleration is the slope of the velocity-time graph. “Average” acceleration would be the slope from the beginning to the end of the graph, disregarding what’s in between. That’s the slope from (0, −3) to (10, 3) which is 6/10 = 0.6 m/$s^{2}$.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_18",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 17–18: A cart moves along a straight road according to the velocity-time graph shown above.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_18\" id=\"ch19p_18\">18.</a></strong> What is the average velocity of this car between time 0 and time 10 s?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>1.2 m/s</p>",
          "<p>24 m/s</p>",
          "<p>12 m/s</p>",
          "<p>2.4 m/s</p>",
          "<p>1.0 m/s</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_18\" id=\"rch19p_18\">18.</a></strong> <strong>A—</strong>Average velocity is defined as displacement divided by time interval. Displacement is found from the area under a velocity-time graph. Here, the areas below and above the $t$-axis in the first 6 seconds cancel. The remaining area is the rectangle (4 s)(3 m/s) = 12 m. Divide by the time interval of 10 s to get 1.2 m/s.</p>"
      },

How far apart are the cars at time $t$ = 4 s?</p>",
        "options": [

          "<p>12 m</p>",
          "<p>4 m</p>"

        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_19\" id=\"rch19p_19\">19.</a></strong> <strong>D—</strong>The distance traveled by each car is found by taking the area under the graph. That’s 8 m for Car A and 4 m for Car B. Car A’s graph is above the horizontal axis, while car B’s graph is below the horizontal axis; this means the cars move in different directions.         "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 20–22: A string of length $L$ is attached to an object of unknown mass. On the surface of Planet X, what is the time for the object to first reach the vertical position?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>$t_{e}$</p>",
          "<p>2$t_{e}$</p>",

          "<p>4$t_{e}$</p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0307-08.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>"
        ],

        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_20\" id=\"rch19p_20\">20.</a></strong> <strong>E—</strong>The time we’re talking about is ¼ of a period. The period of a pendulum equation has $g$ in the denominator and under the square root. The gravitational field on Planet X is ½ that of Earth, so the period of the pendulum there is 1/(1/<img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/root2.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/>) times the period on Earth; that’s the same thing as <img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/root2.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/> times the period on Earth.</p>"
      },

Here $g$ is in the numerator and under the square root.         "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",

        "question": "<p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0308-03.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_23\" id=\"ch19p_23\">23.</a></strong> A ball is dropped from a skyscraper. Between the time of the drop and the time at which the ball reaches terminal velocity, which of the following is true about the magnitudes of the ball’s velocity and acceleration vectors?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>velocity remains constant while acceleration remains constant</p>",
          "<p>velocity increases while acceleration decreases</p>",
          "<p>velocity decreases while acceleration decreases</p>",
          "<p>velocity increases while acceleration remains constant</p>",
          "<p>velocity remains constant while acceleration decreases</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_23\" id=\"rch19p_23\">23.</a></strong> <strong>B—</strong>Terminal velocity is when the ball falls at constant speed because the forces of gravity and air resistance balance. Before reaching terminal velocity, though, the ball had to speed up from rest to reach that speed—so velocity increased. And acceleration is the change in speed every second. Initially the ball was changing speed; once the ball hit terminal velocity, the speed was not changing. The acceleration was nonzero and then zero. So acceleration decreased.</p>"

Use energy conservation: ($M_{1} +M_{2}$)<em>gh</em> = ½($M_{1} +M_{2}$)$v^{2}$. Solve for $v$, and the masses cancel.</p>"

        "id": "ap-mock-physc-mech-3_mc_26",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Mechanics",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_26\" id=\"ch19p_26\">26.</a></strong> A hoop of mass $m$ is released from rest at the top of a ramp, a vertical distance $h$ above the bottom of the ramp. The hoop rolls without slipping to the bottom of the ramp, where it has speed $v$ and total mechanical energy $E$. Next, a solid disk, also of mass $m$, <em></em>is released from the same position, and likewise rolls without slipping. Which of the following is correct about the speed and mechanical energy of the disk compared to the hoop?</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0309-12.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
        "options": [
          "Speed: Disk is faster than hoop; Mechanical Energy: Disk equals hoop",
          "Speed: Disk is faster than hoop; Mechanical Energy: Disk is greater than hoop",
          "Speed: Disk equals hoop; Mechanical Energy: Disk equals hoop",
          "Speed: Disk is slower than hoop; Mechanical Energy: Disk equals hoop",
          "Speed: Disk is slower than hoop; Mechanical Energy: Disk is less than hoop"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_26\" id=\"rch19p_26\">26.</a></strong> <strong>A—</strong>The mechanical energy of the object-Earth systems starts at <em>mgh</em>, and since no work is done by external forces on the objects, the mechanical energy is the same at the bottom as at the top. But that mechanical energy at the bottom consists of both rotational and translational kinetic energies. Since a hoop has mass distributed farther on average from the axis of rotation, the hoop must have a greater rotational inertia. Therefore, a greater proportion of its mechanical energy is rotational rather than translational, and the hoop moves slower, the disk faster.</p>"
      },

        "options": [

          "Angular Momentum: Decreases; Rotational Kinetic Energy: Conserved",
          "Angular Momentum: Decreases; Rotational Kinetic Energy: Decreases",
          "Angular Momentum: Conserved; Rotational Kinetic Energy: Decreases",
          "Angular Momentum: Increases; Rotational Kinetic Energy: Decreases"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_27\" id=\"rch19p_27\">27.</a></strong> <strong>D—</strong>No external torques act on the two-disk system (only the torque of disk 1 on disk 2 and vice versa). That’s the very definition of when angular momentum is conserved. However, the collision is by definition inelastic because the disks stick together.         "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 28 and 29: Three spheres are arranged in deep space as shown above, far away from any planet or star.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_28\" id=\"ch19p_28\">28.</a></strong> Which of the following diagrams shows the correct relative magnitudes and directions of the forces $F_{C}$ (the gravitational force of sphere C on sphere A) and $F_{B}$ (the gravitational force of sphere B on sphere A)?</p>",
        "options": [

          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0310-04.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0310-05.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",

        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_28\" id=\"rch19p_28\">28.</a></strong> <strong>C—</strong>The gravitational force is always attractive, so both forces act to the right.         "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 28 and 29: Three spheres are arranged in deep space as shown above, far away from any planet or star.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19t.xhtml#rch19p_29\" id=\"ch19p_29\">29.</a></strong> In units of <em>Gm</em><sup>2</sup><em>/x</em><em><sup>2</sup></em>, which of the following represents the net gravitational force of spheres B and C on sphere A?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>7/18</p>",
          "<p>7/3</p>",
          "<p>1/6</p>",
          "<p>4/3</p>",
          "<p>11/18</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "E",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_29\" id=\"rch19p_29\">29.</a></strong> <strong>E—</strong>The expression for the force of sphere B on sphere A is $G$(2$m$)($m$)/(2$x$)<sup>2</sup>. Add the forces together because they act in the same direction; you get (11/18)(<em>Gm</em><sup>2</sup><em>/x</em><sup>2</sup>).</p>"

        "answer": "E",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19p.xhtml#ch19p_33\" id=\"rch19p_33\">33.</a></strong> <strong>E—</strong>Kepler’s law says that the period of an orbit squared is proportional to the radius of the orbit cubed.         "options": [

        "question": "<div class='frq-prompt'><h3>CM 2</h3><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19u.xhtml#rch19q_2\" id=\"ch19q_2\">2.</a></strong> Satellites A and B are in circular orbit around a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$.         "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/t0317-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\"><strong>Time:</strong> 45 minutes. You may refer to the constants sheet and the equation sheet, both of which are found in the appendix. You may use a calculator.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0319-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 1 and 2: The circuit above consists of three capacitors and a battery, which has been connected for a long time.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_1\" id=\"ch19r_1\">1.</a></strong> What is the charge stored on the 6 nF capacitor?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>96 nC</p>",
          "<p>48 nC</p>",
          "<p>432 nC</p>",
          "<p>4 nC</p>",
          "<p>144 nC</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_1\" id=\"rch19r_1\">1.</a></strong> <strong>A—</strong>First, reduce the circuit to its simplest form. The parallel capacitors add algebraically to get an equivalent capacitance of 12 nF. Then the series capacitors add inversely by 1/$C_{eq}$ = 1/$C_{1}$ + 1/$C_{2}$. Add 1/12 and 1/6 to get 1/4 . . . that means the equivalent capacitance of the circuit is 4 nF. Now by $Q$ = <em>CV</em>, the whole circuit stores (4 nF) × (24 V) = 96 nC. Series capacitors each take the same charge as each other; that is ALSO equal to the total charge across the combination. So the 6 nF capacitor takes all 96 nC.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-em-3_mc_2",
        "topic": "AP Physics C: Electricity & Magnetism",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/t0317-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\"><strong>Time:</strong> 45 minutes. You may refer to the constants sheet and the equation sheet, both of which are found in the appendix. You may use a calculator.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0319-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 1 and 2: The circuit above consists of three capacitors and a battery, which has been connected for a long time.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_2\" id=\"ch19r_2\">2.</a></strong> What is the voltage across the 8 nF capacitor?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>2 V</p>",
          "<p>12 V</p>",
          "<p>16 V</p>",
          "<p>8 V</p>",
          "<p>3 V</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_2\" id=\"rch19r_2\">2.</a></strong> <strong>D—</strong>The parallel capacitors take the same voltage as each other. Their equivalent capacitance is 12 nF. Both the voltage across this 12 nF equivalent capacitance and the voltage across the 6 nF capacitor must add to 24 V by Kirchhoff’s loop rule. And series capacitors take the same charge in $Q$ = <em>CV</em>. Solving for voltage, the voltage across each capacitor is <em>Q/C</em>, where $Q$ is the same for each. Even if you got the total charge wrong in question 1, you’ll still see that the bigger capacitor takes the smaller voltage, and by a factor of 2 here since 12 nF is twice 6 nF. The 12 nF equivalent capacitor takes 8 V across it (96 nC/12 nF). This means both of the parallel capacitors also take 8 V.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-physc-em-3_mc_3",

        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0319-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 3 and 4: Two long, straight wires are separated by a distance $d$. The left-hand wire carries a current $I$ directed into the page; the right-hand wire carries a current $I$ directed out of the page. Points R and P are positions in space, located as shown in the diagram.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_3\" id=\"ch19r_3\">3.</a></strong> What is the magnitude of the net magnetic field produced at point P?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0319-03.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0319-04.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0319-05.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0319-06.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0319-07.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_3\" id=\"rch19r_3\">3.</a></strong> <strong>C—</strong>The magnetic field due to a long straight wire is $μ_{0}$<em>I/</em>2<em>πr,</em> where $r$ is the distance from the wire to the point being considered. So for the right-hand wire, $r = d$, and for the left-hand wire, $r$ = 2$d$. The direction of the magnetic field is given by the second right-hand rule: point the thumb with the current, curl the fingers to show the field direction. That’s down the page due to the right-hand wire, up the page due to the left-hand wire. So the magnitudes of the two magnetic fields subtract to the total: $μ_{0}$<em>I/</em>2<em>πd</em> − $μ_{0}$<em>I/</em>2$\\pi$(2$d$) gives choice C.</p>"
      },

The left-hand wire carries a current $I$ directed into the page; the right-hand wire carries a current $I$ directed out of the page.         "options": [
          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/larrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
          "<p>Zero</p>",

          "<p><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/4arrow.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_4\" id=\"rch19r_4\">4.</a></strong> <strong>B—</strong>Use the second right-hand rule: point the thumb with the current, and the fingers show the magnetic field direction. The left-hand wire produces a field down and to the right. The right-hand wire produces a field up and to the left. These fields are of equal magnitude, because the currents are the same and the distances from the wires are the same. So the magnetic fields subtract to a net of zero.</p>"

Next, an electron initially moving right with identical speed $v$ enters the magnetic field from the same position.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_5\" id=\"ch19r_5\">5.</a></strong> Which of the labeled positions is closest to where the electron will exit the magnetic field?</p>",

          "<p>X</p>"
        ],

        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_5\" id=\"rch19r_5\">5.</a></strong> <strong>C—</strong>Apply net$F$ = <em>ma</em> in circular motion. Here the net force on the object is <em>qvB</em>, and the acceleration in a circular path is $v^{2}$/$r$. Solve for $r$ to get $r$ = <em>mv/qB</em>. The electron and proton experience the same magnetic field $B$, the same speed $v$, and have the same amount of charge $q$. The difference is, the mass of a proton is something like 2000 times that of the electron. So the radius of the proton’s circular motion will be 2000 times bigger. The only position close to showing an orbital radius 2000 times smaller for the electron is C.</p>"

        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0321-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 9 and 10 refer to the circuit above.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_9\" id=\"ch19r_9\">9.</a></strong> What is the resistance of $R_{2}$?</p>",

Set 100 V = (3 A)($R_{2}$) and solve for $R_{2}$ = 33 Ω.</p>"

But the fundamental equation for capacitors says that $Q$ = <em>CV</em>. So, substitute $V$ = <em>Q/C</em> into the standard expression. You’re left with ½$Q^{2}$/$C$.</p>"

        "question": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_14\" id=\"ch19r_14\">14.</a></strong> Consider a long, straight wire of circular cross section. The current through the wire has uniform current density across its cross-sectional area. Let the distance from the center of the wire along a cross-sectional slice be $r$. The magnetic field inside the wire is proportional to which of the following?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>$r^{2}$</p>",
          "<p>$r$<sup>1/2</sup></p>",
          "<p>$r$</p>",
          "<p>$r^{-}\\$2</p>",
          "<p>$r^{-}\\$1</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_14\" id=\"rch19r_14\">14.</a></strong> <strong>C—</strong>The symmetry is appropriate for Ampere’s law. Never evaluate the integral in Ampere’s law—it always simplifies to <em>BL</em> = $μ_{0} I_{enclosed}$. Here $L$ is the circumference of an amperian loop, 2<em>πr</em>. The current enclosed by this loop is a fraction of the total current. What fraction? A fraction equal to the area enclosed by the amperian loop over the total cross-sectional area of the wire. That’s <em>πr</em><sup>2</sup> over the total area of the wire. Point is, Ampere’s law looks like $B$(2<em>πr</em>) = $μ_{0}$(<em>πr</em><sup>2</sup>/total area)(total $I$ ). Solving for $B$, you’re left with an expression with $r$ by itself in the numerator. So the magnetic field is proportional to $r$. (You’ve memorized the equation $B = μ_{0} I$/2<em>πr</em>, but that’s for the magnetic field <em>outside</em> a long straight wire. This question is asking about $B$ inside the wire.)</p>"

The work done by a uniform force is equal to force times distance, where that distance must be parallel (or antiparallel) to the direction of the force. The electric force is to the right; the force on a positive charge is likewise to the right. So the necessary distance is horizontal only . . . that’s (3 m) (cos 45<sup>o</sup>) = 2.1 m. The work done is (0.40 N) × (2.1 m) = 0.84 J. That work is positive because the electric force is parallel, not antiparallel, to the component of displacement along the direction of force.</p>"

The fingers point into the page at point P. Similarly, the right charge can be thought of as a flow of negative charge up the page, and so is equivalent to a flow of positive charge down the page. Then the electric field due to a charge points away from a positive, toward a negative charge. At point P that’s to the right due to the left-hand charge, and also to the right due to the right-hand charge, making the net electric field to the right.</p>"

        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_22\" id=\"rch19r_22\">22.</a></strong> <strong>A—</strong>The kinetic energy gained by the proton is equal to the potential energy lost from A to B. The potential energy lost by the proton is $q$Δ$V$, where the change in electric potential Δ$V$ is <em>Ed</em> (derived from the equation for a uniform electric field, $E$ = Δ$V$/Δ$x$). The charge $q$ here is the charge of a proton; the distance $d$ is the distance from point A to point P, 0.08 m. Not the distance between plates, but the distance the proton moves! So the change in potential energy is (1.6 × 10<sup>-</sup>19 C)(80 N/C)(0.08 m) = 1.0 × 10<sup>-</sup>18 J.</p>"

The spheres initially each carried positive charge +<em>Q,</em> but have been in electrical contact by means of a long metal wire for a long time.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_23\" id=\"ch19r_23\">23.</a></strong> A rectangular wire loop is located above a wire carrying a current $I$, which increases with time $t$ according to the equation $I$ = 3$t$. Which of the following is correct about the current induced in the wire loop?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>It is counterclockwise and increasing.</p>",
          "<p>It is clockwise and increasing.</p>",

        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_23\" id=\"rch19r_23\">23.</a></strong> <strong>D—</strong>Induced current in the loop is, by Ohm’s law, the induced voltage (EMF) divided by the constant resistance of the loop. So whether induced current is constant depends on the EMF. Induced EMF is <em>dB/dt</em>. The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire depends linearly on $I$. The time derivative of $I$ is a constant value. Thus, the EMF is constant, and so is the induced current. Now, the direction of the magnetic field inside the wire is into the page by the second right-hand rule—point the thumb left with the current producing the field, the fingers curl into the page. This magnetic field is increasing because the current is increasing. So by Lenz’s law, increasing flux is into the page, making decreasing flux out of the page . . . and the induced current is found by pointing the right thumb with decreasing flux and curling the fingers. That’d be counterclockwise.</p>"

The spheres initially each carried positive charge +<em>Q,</em> but have been in electrical contact by means of a long metal wire for a long time.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_24\" id=\"ch19r_24\">24.</a></strong> Which of the following statements is true about the electric potential at the center of each sphere?</p>",

But that potential isn’t zero! The electric potential is considered zero a long way away from any charges. Since these spheres have positive charge, they create positive potential outside of the spheres, and so they must have a uniform but positive potential everywhere inside.</p>"

        "question": "<p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0325-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_26\" id=\"ch19r_26\">26.</a></strong> Circuit 1 above shows three identical resistors labeled X, Y, and Z. In circuit 2, resistor Z is removed. Which of the following correctly compares the current through and voltage across resistor Y in circuit 2 compared to circuit 1?</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0325-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0325-03.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
        "options": [
          "Current through Y: Greater; Voltage across Y: Greater",
          "Current through Y: Smaller; Voltage across Y: Smaller",

          "Current through Y: Unchanged; Voltage across Y: Unchanged"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_26\" id=\"rch19r_26\">26.</a></strong> <strong>A—</strong>First, consider the whole circuit: the battery is the same, so the total voltage is unchanged. The equivalent resistance increases because we removed a parallel branch. By $V$ = <em>IR</em>, the total current must decrease. Now apply Ohm’s law to resistor X only: The reduced total current all runs through resistor X, but resistor X can’t change its own resistance. So by $V$ = <em>IR</em>, the voltage across bulb X is smaller than before. Kirchoff’s loop rule says that the voltage across X and Y must sum to V. . . so with smaller voltage across X, there must be greater voltage across Y. Now apply Ohm’s law to bulb Y: greater voltage with unchanged resistance means greater current, too.</p>"

        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background: rgba(255,255,255,0.03); padding: 12px 16px; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 14px; border-left: 3px solid #7c3aed;\"><p class=\"noindent\">Questions 27 and 28: The diagram above shows two concentric spherical conducting shells. The net charge on the inner sphere is −2$Q$. The net charge on the outer sphere is +3$Q$.</p></div><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_27\" id=\"ch19r_27\">27.</a></strong> What is the charge that resides on the outer surface of the outer shell?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<p>+2$Q$</p>",
          "<p>zero</p>",
          "<p>$+Q$</p>",
          "<p>+3$Q$</p>",
          "<p>+5$Q$</p>"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_27\" id=\"rch19r_27\">27.</a></strong> <strong>C—</strong>The electric field inside a conductor is zero; charge can only sit on the surface of a conductor. Consider a Gaussian surface drawn inside the outer shell, going through point C. Since the shell is conducting, there must be zero electric field inside. Therefore, this Gaussian surface must enclose zero total charge. The inner shell contains charge −2$Q$, so the inner surface of the outer shell—the part inside this Gaussian surface—contains +2$Q$ to make the total charge inside the Gaussian surface zero. Then the remaining +1$Q$ of charge on the outer shell must be on the outer surface.</p>"

        "topic": "AP Physics C: Electricity & Magnetism",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0326-06.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19v.xhtml#rch19r_33\" id=\"ch19r_33\">33.</a></strong> An electron is initially moving to the left with speed $v$ parallel to a wire carrying a constant rightward current $I$ as shown above. Which of the following indicates the direction of the magnetic force on the electron at the instant shown, and whether the long-term path of the electron is circular or not circular?</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/f0326-07.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
        "options": [
          "Direction of Force: Upward (away from wire); Path: Circular",
          "Direction of Force: Upward (away from wire); Path: Not circular",
          "Direction of Force: Zero; Path: Straight line",
          "Direction of Force: Downward (toward wire); Path: Circular",
          "Direction of Force: Downward (toward wire); Path: Not circular"
        ],
        "answer": "E",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong><a href=\"ch19r.xhtml#ch19r_33\" id=\"rch19r_33\">33.</a></strong> <strong>E—</strong>The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire is given by the second right-hand rule: Point the thumb to the right and curl. The fingers point out of the page above the wire, so that’s the direction of the magnetic field. Now the force on the electron is given by the first right-hand rule: Point with the velocity, curl the fingers out of the page with the magnetic field, and the thumb gives the upward force on a positive charge. An electron has a negative charge, though, so the force is downward. Because the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, the path is initially circular. But because the magnetic field isn’t uniform (it drops off the farther you get from the current-carrying wire), the magnetic force isn’t always of the same magnitude, and so the path becomes not circular.</p>"
      },

        "question": "A loop is moved out of a magnetic field at constant velocity as shown. Which of the following statements about the induced current in the loop and the applied force on the loop is correct? (The magnetic field points into the page.)",

      {
        "id": "drill_tens_q15",
        "topic": "Tension Dynamics",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p><strong>Tension Drill #15:</strong> Two blocks of mass $M$ and $m$ ($M > m$) hang on opposite sides of a frictionless pulley. If the pulley itself has mass $M_p$ and rotational inertia $I = \\frac{1}{2}M_p R^2$, derive the expression for string tension $T_1$ on mass $M$.</p>",
        "isFRQ": true,
        "rubric": "<p>Setting up equations: $Mg - T_1 = Ma$, $T_2 - mg = ma$, and $(T_1 - T_2)R = I\\alpha = \\frac{1}{2}M_p a$. Adding gives $a = \\frac{(M-m)g}{M + m + M_p/2}$. Substituting gives $T_1 = Mg\\left[\\frac{2m + M_p/2}{M + m + M_p/2}\\right]$.</p>",
        "options": [
          "Submit analytical derivation in workspace."
        ],
        "answer": "FRQ_MANUAL_EVALUATION",
        "explanation": "<p>Accounting for pulley inertia: $T_1 = Mg\\left[\\frac{2m + M_p/2}{M + m + M_p/2}\\right]$.</p>"
      },

      {
        "id": "drill_field_q17",
        "topic": "E&M Fields",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p><strong>Electric and Magnetic Fields Drill #17:</strong> Determine the magnitude and direction of the electric and magnetic forces acting on the particle:</p><p class=\"quesa\"><strong>17.</strong> a positron moving up and to the right, at an angle of 30° to the horizontal, at 2 m/s</p>",
        "isFRQ": true,
        "rubric": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong>17.</strong> <img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0068-12.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><h4 class=\"h4\">Step-by-Step Solution to #2:</h4><p class=\"noindent\">(a) The magnetic force on a charge is given by <em>F</em> = <em>qvB</em> sin <em>θ</em>. Since the velocity is perpendicular to the magnetic field, <em>θ</em> = 90°, and sin <em>θ</em> = 1. The charge <em>q</em> is the amount of charge on an electron, 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C. <em>v</em> is the electron’s speed, 2 m/s. <em>B</em> is the magnetic field, 3 T.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0068-13.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">The direction is given by the right-hand rule. Point your fingers in the direction of the electron’s velocity, toward the top of the page; curl your fingers in the direction of the magnetic field, to the right; your thumb points into the page. Since the electron has a negative charge, the force points opposite your thumb, or out of the page.</p><p class=\"noindentt\">(b) Even though we’re dealing with a magnetic force, we can still use Newton’s second law. Since the magnetic force is the only force acting, just set this force equal to <em>ma</em> and solve. The direction of the acceleration must be in the same direction as the net force.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0068-14.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><h4 class=\"h4\">Step-by-Step Solution to #10:</h4><p class=\"noindent\">(a) The electric force on a charge is given by <em>F</em> = <em>qE</em>. The charge <em>q</em> is the amount of charge on an electron, 1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C. <em>E</em> is the electric field, 3 N/C.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0069-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Because the electron has a negative charge, the force is opposite the electric field, or right.</p><p class=\"noindentt\">(b) Even though we’re dealing with an electric force, we can still use Newton’s second law. Since the electric force is the only force acting, just set this force equal to <em>ma</em> and solve. The direction of the acceleration must be in the same direction as the net force.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0069-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>",
        "options": [
          "Submit analytical / algebraic result in workspace."
        ],
        "answer": "FRQ_MANUAL_EVALUATION",
        "explanation": "<p class=\"ques\"><strong>17.</strong> <img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0068-12.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><h4 class=\"h4\">Step-by-Step Solution to #2:</h4><p class=\"noindent\">(a) The magnetic force on a charge is given by $F$ = <em>qvB</em> sin $\\theta$. Since the velocity is perpendicular to the magnetic field, $\\theta$ = 90°, and sin $\\theta$ = 1. The charge $q$ is the amount of charge on an electron, 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C. $v$ is the electron’s speed, 2 m/s. $B$ is the magnetic field, 3 T.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0068-13.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">The direction is given by the right-hand rule. Point your fingers in the direction of the electron’s velocity, toward the top of the page; curl your fingers in the direction of the magnetic field, to the right; your thumb points into the page. Since the electron has a negative charge, the force points opposite your thumb, or out of the page.</p><p class=\"noindentt\">(b) Even though we’re dealing with a magnetic force, we can still use Newton’s second law. Since the magnetic force is the only force acting, just set this force equal to <em>ma</em> and solve. The direction of the acceleration must be in the same direction as the net force.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0068-14.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><h4 class=\"h4\">Step-by-Step Solution to #10:</h4><p class=\"noindent\">(a) The electric force on a charge is given by $F$ = <em>qE</em>. The charge $q$ is the amount of charge on an electron, 1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C. $E$ is the electric field, 3 N/C.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0069-01.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p><p class=\"noindent\">Because the electron has a negative charge, the force is opposite the electric field, or right.</p><p class=\"noindentt\">(b) Even though we’re dealing with an electric force, we can still use Newton’s second law. Since the electric force is the only force acting, just set this force equal to <em>ma</em> and solve. The direction of the acceleration must be in the same direction as the net force.</p><p class=\"image\"><img alt=\"Images\" class=\"q-img\" src=\"images/e0069-02.jpg\" style=\"max-width: 100%; height: auto; margin: 10px 0; display: block;\"/></p>"
      },

        "question": "<p>A spherical balloon is being inflated at a rate of 3 cubic inches per second.         "options": [
          "0.010 inches per second",
          "0.120 inches per second",
          "1.667 inches per second",
          "3.000 inches per second"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<strong>A</strong> <p>This is a related rates\r                                 question because you’re being asked to relate the rate of change in\r                                 the volume (how fast the balloon is being inflated) to the rate of\r                                 change in the radius. This means you take the derivative of the\r                                 equation that relates volume and radius, which is <img src=\"images/f7bc231d2c584d6ea17aec6d0fc457bb.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">.</p> <p>The rates of change are\r                                 given by the derivatives, so differentiate both sides of the\r                                 equation:</p> <p><img src=\"images/fd1865ed71444822bb7c004c85247cf8.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>The problem is asking\r                                 for the rate of change of the radius, or <img src=\"images/d113a309ad634410a91d8ca7841a0397.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, when <em>r</em> = 5, given that the\r                                     rate of change of the volume is <img src=\"images/3c41521370f543a29d1d1c78c753c369.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> = 3. (Pay attention to the units for each number given.\r                                 Cubic inches is a measurement of volume.) Substitute this\r                                 information into the differentiated equation and solve for <img src=\"images/6a9ed1eb94464877abd40597522b1c0f.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">:</p> <p><img src=\"images/e8992b2bea8545bdab3667023615d030.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Use your calculator to\r                                 find that this is approximately 0.010 inches per second, or\r                                  (A).</p>"
      },

        "explanation": "<strong>D</strong>  <p>If <em>u</em> =\r                                 <em>x</em><sup> 2</sup>, then <em>du</em> = 2<em>x</em> <em>dx</em>. This means either (B) or (D) is correct.</p> <p>When looking for the\r                                 equivalent definite integral, don’t forget to convert the limits of\r                                 integration: <em>u</em> = <em>x</em><sup> 2</sup>,\r                                 so <em>u</em> = 0 when <em>x</em> = 0 and <em>u</em> =\r                                 4 when <em>x</em> = 2. Be sure to replace the <em>u</em>-values\r                                 where their corresponding <em>x</em>-values were (<em>x</em> = 2\r                                 was the upper limit so <em>u</em> = 4 is the new upper\r                                 limit).</p> <p>The integral in terms of\r                                 <em>x</em> can now be written in terms of\r                                 <em>u</em> as:</p> <p><img src=\"images/9c205ef4c7db472abe962fcc35a45803.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>That’s (D).</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-3-q12",
        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>Which of the following series converge?</p>",
        "options": [
          "I only",
          "II only",
          "I and II only",
          "II and III only"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<strong>D</strong>  <p>I does not converge by\r                                 the <em>p</em>-series rule.</p> <p>II converges because it\r                                 is a geometric series with a ratio between –1 and 1.</p> <p>III converges because\r                                 the factorial in the denominator makes the ratio test equal zero for\r                                 all values of <em>x</em>.</p> <p>Hence, (D) is the\r                                 correct answer.</p>"
      },

          "<em>x</em>(<em>t</em>) = 2 sin <em>t</em> + 3",

Substitute into the position equation to get:</p> <p><img src=\"images/013141b49a7f41fea1bff600da9c5646.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Hence, the position\r                                 function is <em>x</em>(<em>t</em>) = 2 sin\r                                 <em>t</em> + 3, which is (C).</p>"

What is the value of\r                             <img src=\"images/28f1f653355a4a808ecf94b31c1cfb59.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">\r                             at <em>x</em> = 2 ?</p>",

Once you have finished taking your derivative(s), you can\r                                 then plug in any known values.  It is much easier to do the\r                                 algebra when you have numbers in the equation rather than having to\r                                 deal with many variables.</p> <p>Substitute the values of\r                                 <em>x</em>, <em>y</em>, and <img src=\"images/1e091a5536da47389b925927ca4d5cf3.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> to get:</p> <p><img src=\"images/2727a6f145e74d6a84e6623807c70c88.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>That’s (C).</p>"

      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-3-q16",
        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>The function <em>f</em> has the property that <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>), <em>f′</em>(<em>x</em>), and <em>f″</em>(<em>x</em>) are positive for all <em>x</em> > 0 . Which of the following could be part of the graph of <em>f </em>?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<img src=\"images/chapter29a_ab_pt3_16a.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/chapter29a_ab_pt3_16b.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/chapter29a_ab_pt3_16c.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/chapter29a_ab_pt3_16e.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong>  <p>First, <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) > 0 means that\r                                 <em>f</em> is above the <em>x</em>-axis. All of the choices meet\r                                 this condition (for <em>x </em>> 0 as stipulated in the question\r                                 stem).</p> <p>Second, <em>f′</em>(<em>x</em>) > 0 means that\r                                 <em>f</em> is increasing. This eliminates (B).</p> <p>Third, <em>f″</em>(<em>x</em>) > 0 means that\r                                 <em>f</em> is concave up. This eliminates (A), which is linear so\r                                 it is neither concave up nor, not or down, and (D), which is concave\r                                 down. Thus, the correct answer is (C), which is above the\r                                 <em>x</em>-axis, increasing, and concave up.</p>"

      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-3-q17",
        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background:rgba(124,58,237,0.06); border-left:4px solid #7c3aed; padding:12px 16px; border-radius:8px; margin-bottom:14px;\"><p><img src=\"images/chapter29a_ab_pt3_17.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p></div><p>The graph of a function <em>f</em> is shown above. The area of the region between <em>f</em> and the <em>x</em>-axis on the closed interval [0, 3] is 9 . The area of the region between <em>f</em> and the <em>x</em>-axis on the closed interval [3, 5] is 2 . What is the  value of\r                             <img src=\"images/89d741dcf79c40a8ad339ce6ff22dd37.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "5",
          "7",
          "11",
          "18"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<strong>B</strong>  <p>The reason that the\r                                 integral symbol looks like an elongated <em>S</em> is because the\r                                 definite integral is used to find the sum of an infinite\r                                 number of really, really small terms.  When you are using an\r                                 integral to find the area under a curve, you are adding the areas of\r                                 an infinite number of extremely thin rectangles: area =\r                                 (length)(width) = (<em>y</em>)(<em>dx</em>). The integral from\r                                 <em>x</em> = 0 to <em>x</em> = 3 is positive because the graph\r                                 is above the <em>x</em>-axis, making the <em>y</em>-values\r                                 positive. The integral from <em>x</em> = 3 to\r                                 <em>x</em> = 5 is negative because the graph is below the\r                                 <em>x</em>-axis, making the <em>y</em>-values negative.</p> <p>Thus, (B) is correct\r                                 because:</p> <p><img src=\"images/202a0d5574c24e1b870f42274a49ae4f.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-3-q18",
        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>The line tangent to the graph of\r                             <img src=\"images/eabfb2fa859140eea7e5a02951ef3f4d.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">\r                             is parallel to the line <em>x</em> – 3<em>y</em> = 3 at which of the following?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<em>x</em> = 0 only",
          "<em>x</em> = –2 only",
          "<em>x</em> = –4 and <em>x</em> = –2",
          "<em>x</em> = 0 and <em>x</em> = –6"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<strong>D</strong>  <p>Parallel lines have the\r                                 same slope. To find the slope of the given line, rewrite the\r                                 equation in slope-intercept form:</p> <p><img src=\"images/531779e3be1d4f738f6b73a58e6f5f57.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Thus, the slope of both\r                                 lines is\r                                 <img src=\"images/d711ff08e1d248579e55b9cc70ec810b.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">.</p> <p>To find the slope of\r                                 <em>f</em>, use the quotient rule to differentiate\r                                 <img src=\"images/78df1ea76d19485d930429c902b14751.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">:</p> <p><img src=\"images/677cab9ce9374b75953448d2a0d3826d.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>This needs to equal the\r                                 slope of the other line, so <img src=\"images/95ddeae427fb4675ba6615b54981b1ce.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">.</p> <p>Now solve for <em>x.\r                             </em>Cross-multiply to get 9 = (<em>x</em>\r                                 + 3)<sup>2</sup>. This becomes <em>x</em> + 3 = ±3. So <em>x</em> = –3 ± 3, which\r                                 means <em>x</em> = –6 or\r                                 <em>x</em> = 0. That’s (D).</p>"
      },

      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-3-q20",
        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>Which of the following functions has the line <em>y</em> = 3 as a horizontal asymptote?</p>",
        "options": [
          "I only",
          "I and II only",
          "I and III only",
          "I, II, and III"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong>  <p>Horizontal asymptotes\r                                 occur if the function approaches a particular <em>y-</em>value as\r                                 <em>x</em> → ∞ or <em>x</em> → –∞. When <em>x</em>\r                                 approaches positive or negative infinity, the highest powers of\r                                 <em>x</em> are so much larger than the other <em>x</em>s that you\r                                 can disregard the smaller powers of <em>x</em>.</p> <p>For statement I:</p> <p><img src=\"images/62b52153fdbf4b8dab0054488501e0d0.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>So, <em>y</em> = 3 is a horizontal asymptote.\r                                 Note, as <em>x</em> → –∞, <em>y</em> → –3.</p> <p>For statement II:</p> <p><img src=\"images/4fec37b3b6964f0d9d8c3ce968ad5ff5.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>and</p> <p><img src=\"images/15f7b465b36c4080b101d6047baec3a8.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">,</p> <p>So, <em>y</em> = –3 is a horizontal asymptote,\r                                 but <em>y</em> = 3 is not, so eliminate\r                                 (B) and (D).</p> <p>For statement III:</p> <p><img src=\"images/674d87f1c6dd46b797d38c6ee5acb0de.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>So, <em>y</em> = 3 is a horizontal asymptote.\r                                  You would get the same asymptote if <em>x</em> → –∞.</p> <p>Thus, I and III have\r                                 <em>y</em> = 3 as horizontal\r                                 asymptotes, making (C) the correct answer.</p>"
      },

        "options": [

This means (A) is correct.</p>"

        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<div class=\"passage-box\" style=\"background:rgba(124,58,237,0.06); border-left:4px solid #7c3aed; padding:12px 16px; border-radius:8px; margin-bottom:14px;\"><p><img src=\"images/chapter29a_ab_pt3_24.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p></div><p>A slope field for which of the following differential equations is shown above?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<img src=\"images/920487343c1642bba2f91bc11e4a185a.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/2bf4624d459b4cd79866c1dcdd5a485b.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/65176c12ba0942448feea665d8346aaf.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/63a829f4d9544d448c4452e7d0eaebf2.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<strong>A</strong>  <p>Each tangent line has\r                                 the same slope,\r                                 <img src=\"images/4803832773df40e68d39db52eb3f7e70.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, for any given value of <em>y</em>, so the slope only depends\r                                 on <em>y </em>(to see this, notice that all the slopes that are\r                                 horizontal to one another are the same). Thus, the slopes are not\r                                 affected by the <em>x</em>-values, so the differential equation should\r                                 only be in terms of the variable <em>y</em>. This eliminates (C) and\r                                 (D).</p> <p>Now, you might notice\r                                 that the slope field has horizontal tangent lines at <em>y</em> = –2, so the slope,\r                                 <img src=\"images/1a90bb3985f94087b02579adc872ba09.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, must equal 0 when <em>y</em> =\r                                     –2. Unfortunately, that is true for both (A) and (B), so\r                                 that doesn’t help narrow down the choices.</p> <p>To decide between (A)\r                                 and (B), choose simple values (ones that are easy to find on the\r                                 graph), like <em>x</em> = 0 and <em>y</em> = 0, to plug into the\r                                 equation. These are nice values because they lie on the axes.\r                                 Looking along the <em>x</em>-axis of the graph, the slope is negative\r                                 when <em>y</em> = 0. So (A) must be correct.</p>"

        "difficulty": "medium",

For the second\r                                 factor, 2<em>e<sup>t</sup></em> = 1.\r                                 Solving for <em>t</em> gives\r                                 <img src=\"images/f3e730a18a914da49e0bbc83d9cff131.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">\r                                 or\r                                 <img src=\"images/3985c3731fea42f19367a05ac6292060.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. Make sure you answer the\r                                 question asked.</p> <p>The acceleration at this\r                                 time is:</p> <p><img src=\"images/79711205975a49a3a7d14841a019572a.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p>\r                             Thus, (A) is correct."

      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-3-q33",
        "topic": "Section I: Part B (Calculator Active)",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p>Suppose a function <em>f</em> is continuous for all <em>x </em>. If <em>f</em> has a relative minimum at (–2, –3) and a relative maximum at (4, 5), which of the following statements must be true?</p>",
        "options": [
          "The graph of <em>f</em> has an absolute maximum at (4, 5).",
          "The graph of <em>f</em> is increasing for all <em>x</em> in –2 < <em>x</em> < 4.",
          "There exists some <em>c</em> in the interval –2 < <em>x</em> < 4 such that <em>f</em>(c) = 0.",
          "There exists some <em>c</em> in the interval –2 < <em>x</em> < 4 such that <em>f′</em>(c) = 0."
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong>  <p>Compare each statement\r                                 to what you’re given in the question. Start with (A): The function\r                                 <em>f</em> does not have to have an absolute extremum, not\r                                 extrema. That is only guaranteed if the function is continuous on a\r                                 <em>closed</em> interval, so eliminate (A).</p> <p>(B): The graph of\r                                 <em>f</em> could be increasing for all <em>x</em> in –2 < <em>x</em> < 4, but it does not\r                                 have to be. There could be other extrema and thus other turning\r                                 points between <em>x</em> = –2 and <em>x</em> =\r                                 4. Eliminate (B).</p> <p>(C): The statement\r                                 <em>f</em>(<em>c</em>) = 0 means there is a <em>y</em>-value equal to\r                                 0 for some <em>x</em>-value equal to <em>c</em>. Because <em>y</em> =\r                                 0 is between <em>y</em> = –3 and <em>y</em>  = 5, this\r                                 statement must be true by the intermediate value theorem,\r                                 so (C) is correct.</p> <p>There is no need to\r                                 check (D), but in case you’re not sure about (C), you can eliminate\r                                 (D) because the function <em>f</em> could be strictly increasing\r                                 for <em>x</em> between –2 and 4, in which case <em>f'</em>(<em>x</em>) is\r                                 always positive (not 0). Note that the only time <em>f'</em>(<em>c</em>)\r                                 is guaranteed to be 0 is (by Rolle’s theorem) when <em>f</em> is\r                                 continuous and differentiable and the <em>y</em>-values are the same\r                                 at the endpoints.</p>"

        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-3-q34",
        "topic": "Section I: Part B (Calculator Active)",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p>The growth of a population <em>P</em> is modeled by the differential equation\r                             <img src=\"images/63fae823edab4a1bba690d5da0e37f04.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. If the population is 2 at <em>t</em> = 0, what is the population at <em>t</em> = 5 ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "5.565",
          "20.401",
          "50.810",
          "70.679"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<strong>D</strong>  <p>This differential\r                                 equation is of the form\r                                 <img src=\"images/8f4373b042bd43e48afeef622c926141.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, where the rate of change is proportional to the amount\r                                 present. This means that the population’s growth can be modeled by a\r                                 typical exponential equation of the form <em>P</em> =\r                                 <em>P</em><sub>0</sub><em>e</em><sup><em>kt</em></sup>.\r                                 Using <em>P</em><sub>0</sub> = 2 (the initial population at time\r                                 = 0) and <em>k</em> = 0.713,\r                                 this model becomes <em>P</em> =\r                                 2<em>e</em><sup>0.713<em>t</em></sup>.         "question": "<p>The number of bacteria in a petri dish increases at a rate of <em>R</em>(<em>t</em>) bacteria per hour. If there are 1,000 bacteria at time <em>t</em> = 5, which of the following expressions gives the total number of bacteria in the petri dish at <em>t</em> = 7 ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<em>\r                                 R</em>(7)",
          "1,000 + <em>R</em>(7)",
          "<img src=\"images/062fc29086594b6797e73e84d34285b9.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/4751b951e69f4918866077d3b5bf25b8.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong> <p>For you to find the\r                                 total number of bacteria in the petri dish, you must add the number\r                                 of new bacteria (those added from <em>t</em> = 5 to <em>t</em> = 7) to\r                                 the number of bacteria at time <em>t</em> = 5. The answer is <img src=\"images/5f3eafed6efb4aada60e6a21f042aa8e.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. The 1,000 represents the starting number of bacteria, and\r                                 the <img src=\"images/142f212ece7047d38e74f04f5865aaea.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> represents the additional bacteria.</p> <p>Hence, (C) is correct.\r                                 (A) is the rate at which the number of bacteria is changing at time\r                                     <em>t</em> = 7 and does not represent the total number of\r                                 bacteria. If the question asked for how many bacteria grow from\r                                     <em>t</em> = 5 to <em>t</em> = 7, (D) would have been correct.</p>"

      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-4-q2",
        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>Which of the following sequences does not converge?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<img src=\"images/bf8d1eb753be4ea5b7ddc767f4923f4c.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/eb96cb03e9e1440689ef220ca58cfddd.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/02280b03104c4e47995a3ab73af4096c.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/0a7f6df122564c08805a3bf16943e49a.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong> <p>Deciding if a sequence\r                                 converges as<em> n</em> gets infinitely large is like deciding if a\r                                 finite limit exists for a function as <em>x </em>approaches infinity.\r                                 The sequence <img src=\"images/ad78e5cc00b546ab8119908f0a3d73ab.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> continues to oscillate between positive and negative numbers\r                                 as <em>n</em> continues to get larger, so it does not converge.</p> <p>Therefore, (C) is\r                                 correct. Even though the numerator in (A) seems like a large value,\r                                 it is still a constant. As <em>n</em> gets infinitely large, <img src=\"images/102fd16ad397489088733122dd61f900.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> converges to 0 because the denominator will eventually grow\r                                 larger than the numerator. (B) can be written as <img src=\"images/14663f9f57f74f649cabc30a889305d5.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. Because the numerator and denominator have the same degree,\r                                 the sequence converges to the ratio of the leading coefficients,\r                                 which is 4. (D) can be rewritten as <img src=\"images/143f3b52e12d4e9f853f34c53d06507c.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> When the sequence is defined by a rational expression and\r                                 the degree of the denominator is greater than the degree of the\r                                 numerator, the sequence converges to 0.</p>"
      },

Because <img src=\"images/145f7db234df4943b8c6ddd52cb36d49.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> is tangent to <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) at <em>x</em> = 3, you can\r                                 find <em>f</em>(3) by evaluating <em>y</em>(3).</p> <p><img src=\"images/832307ab049d463a8f50f513b033d949.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>The point (3, 7) and the\r                                 slope <img src=\"images/e4e64204e355460bb0c32381b03532d3.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> can now be put into the point-slope form of a line.</p> <p><img src=\"images/213dbf6ff624481b869898f129a2b360.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Thus, (C) is correct.\r                                 (A) uses the reciprocal slope of the tangent line instead of the\r                                 negative reciprocal. (B) uses the correct slope but incorrectly\r                                 distributes the slope when working with the point-slope form of a\r                                 line.</p>"

        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<strong>D</strong> <p>To find the area between\r                                 the function and the <em>x</em>-axis, it is easier to have a picture\r                                 or sketch of the function in order to properly write the integral\r                                 that represents the area.</p>  <img src=\"images/chapter28_a-106.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">  <p>As shown in the sketch,\r                                 this function is a negative quadratic function translated 16 units\r                                 up as compared to the parent function. To evaluate the integral, first take the antiderivative.\r                                 Then find the difference between the upper and lower bounds.</p> <p><img src=\"images/ce87eb2789614814ace350e84cf83431.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Therefore, (D) is\r                                 correct. Use the trigonometric identity sin<sup>2</sup><em>x</em> +\r                                     cos<sup>2</sup><em>x</em> = 1 to replace denominator with <img src=\"images/3debe6fdef2341889865f5edd3af4016.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> . Then evaluate the limit as <em>x</em> approaches 0. You are\r                                 left with <img src=\"images/44c5c935b4bd4423b9ecf6491f720e9b.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, which equals –5. Substituting into the point-slope formula for the\r                                     equation of a line yields <em>y</em> – 1 = 3.464(<em>x</em> –\r                                     2.732).</p> <p>Therefore, (D) is\r                                     correct.
