The next coordinate is reached by calculating\r                                     the Δ<em>y </em>at <em>x</em> = 0.</p> <p><img src=\"images/966a7b8286844f41b6988cc007720f13.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Then add <img src=\"images/906d345f592945e189244b66a63474fa.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> to (0, 7.18) to get the new point, (0.3, 7.69). The next\r                                     and final coordinate is reached by calculating the Δ<em>y</em> at\r                                         <em>x</em> = 0.3.</p> <p><img src=\"images/208ccf68605d47f899a5f8340ce1e67c.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Then add <img src=\"images/ee1c7afd4fac4642b82268f22ac1a14e.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> to (0.3, 7.69) to get the new point, (0.6, 8.32).         "topic": "Section I: Part B (Calculator Active)",
        "difficulty": "hard",

Lastly, to find the coordinates in polar form,(<em>r</em>,\r                                         <em>$\\theta$</em>) simply plug the <em>$\\theta$</em> value into the original\r                                     equation <em>r </em>= 2 + 3 cos (<em>$\\theta$</em>). Thus, (D) is\r                                     correct.</p> <p>(A), (B), and (C)\r                                     are all points at which the tangent line is horizontal. (B) is the\r                                 derivative of the partial sum formula evaluated at <em>n</em> = 5.</p>"

If the\r                             5th-degree Taylor polynomial for <em>f</em> about <em>x</em> = 0 is used to\r                             approximate <img src=\"images/974dca31b84b4e0b94de50453c768cc6.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, what is the alternating series error bound?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<img src=\"images/dc82788f7bcb424d9708622aa73764d8.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "<img src=\"images/2ffd30e9d8ef41008adf8fdbde243538.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",

        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong> <p>The alternating series\r                                 error bound formula can be used to find the amount of error in the\r                                 approximation of a power series versus the actual function in an\r                                 alternating series by taking the absolute values of the next omitted\r                                 term. The formula for the alternating series error bound is <img src=\"images/e832ecd6187b4056bdd34569be1fe36f.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> where the error is less than the absolute value of the next\r                                 term. Since the polynomial was a 5th degree, as shown in the series\r                                 formula, a fifth degree polynomial would be created when <em>n</em> =\r                                 2. To find the alternating series error bound, you take the absolute\r                                 value of the next term, in this case <em>n</em> = 3. For <em>n</em> = 3\r                                 and <img src=\"images/7542d6bcb30a48769ad46e67efd58d5a.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, use the alternating series error bound formula.</p> <p><img src=\"images/6e5aab13fd694a4c9843b16766d9b7c4.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Hence, (C) is correct.\r                                 (A) fails to use the absolute value at the end and keeps the\r                                 difference negative. This is not a correct usage of the alternating\r                                 series error bound formula. (B) uses <em>n</em> = 6, which would form\r                                 a 13-degree polynomial. (D) is missing the exponent on the base 2 in\r                                 the denominator.</p>"

        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong> <p>This differential\r                                 equation is defined by both <em>x</em> and <em>y</em>. (B) would be correct if the given condition had a negative\r                                     <em>y</em>-value.</p>"

Each vertical distance traveled by the ball is\r                                 defined by <img src=\"images/216a409bc6104cea8d442a73f960ef6c.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. The scenario can be represented by the series</p> <p><img src=\"images/18aeb68e3d274110bf0925e1421e82f4.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>which can be simplified\r                                 to <img src=\"images/a0edacfdcf7d42de96d483c74e05451a.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> If the initial 12 is rewritten as –12 + 24, the series\r                                 becomes <img src=\"images/a3440b75f0a649a3a406803e9d1fd3fd.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> and can be written in the familiar geometric form <img src=\"images/ce9050d2665449d7905a4285dceb3475.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. The sum of a geometric series with <img src=\"images/677a7121d4014f17abb25d6ed8d9c997.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> is <img src=\"images/a65bfdd4288840b4b173167e2bf2f8d6.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. In this situation, that becomes <img src=\"images/44abaa597d804bb5aeb9693a756e1a35.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. Don’t forget to add the –12 to this sum, giving you a total\r                                 vertical distance of 36 meters.</p> <p>Hence, (B) is correct.\r                                 (A) is <img src=\"images/c4534bd51ed44d96b5191ab35e482f57.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, which does not account for the ball traveling the same\r                                 vertical distance twice after the initial drop. (C) is just <img src=\"images/0b58ea8c1249430e8b28cdf26a771730.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">.</p>"

        "question": "<p>Consider the curve <em>y</em>\r                             = –<em>x</em><sup>3</sup> + 5<em>x</em> +1. Find an equation for the tangent\r                             to the curve at the point (2, 3) .</p>",

        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>Let <em>f</em> and <em>g</em>\r                             be differentiable functions with <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) < 0 for all of\r                                 <em>x</em> and <em>g</em>(0) = 2.</p>",

        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong> <p>The function\r                                     <em>h</em>(<em>x</em>) is defined as the quotient of two\r                                 differentiable functions, and the derivative of <em>h</em>(<em>x</em>)\r                                 is provided. Using the quotient rule, you can compare the actual\r                                 derivative to what you get when following the rule.</p> <p><img src=\"images/72c7a32fcec64fb4b90d1311be3f801f.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>You can see the given\r                                 numerator is missing the second term from the quotient rule, meaning\r                                 the second term must be equal to 0. For <em>g</em><em>′</em>(<em>x</em>)\r                                     <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) to equal 0, either<em> f</em>(<em>x</em>) = 0\r                                     or<em> g</em><em>′</em>(<em>x</em>) = 0. The derivative of a constant is 0, making\r                                 <em>g</em>(<em>x</em>) a constant.         "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>What is the average value of\r                                 <img src=\"images/daf5fb4e51094a9482a88c83dd151133.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> on the closed interval [1, 4] ?</p>",

        "explanation": "<strong>B</strong> <p>Using the average value\r                                 theorem, you get the following.</p> <p><img src=\"images/eea4d35006174e7f82cdcde2e9570578.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Hence, (B) is correct.\r                                 (A) is the mean value of the function on the same interval. (D) is missing the <img src=\"images/cc6a657674854b258b10d09d89e9ade5.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> portion of the theorem.</p>"

        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>Which of the following is\r                             the average rate of change of the function <img src=\"images/21dbbfb975b24da190e9325c42f61148.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> over the closed interval [0, 1] ?</p>",

        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong> <p>The average rate of\r                                 change is the same as the slope of the secant line between <em>x</em>\r                                 = 0 and <em>x</em> = 1.       {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-6-q22",
        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>Let <em>f</em> be the function\r                             given by <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) = <em>x</em><sup>3</sup> –\r                                 6<em>x</em><sup>2</sup>. What are all values of <em>c</em> that satisfy\r                             the conclusion of the mean value theorem of differential calculus on the\r                             closed interval [0, 6] ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "0 only",
          "4 only",
          "0 and 4",
          "4 and 6"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<strong>B</strong> <p>The mean value theorem\r                                 requires you to find the corresponding <em>y</em>-coordinates of the\r                                 given endpoints of the domain in question: <em>f</em>(0) = 0 and\r                                     <em>f</em>(6) = 0. Setting the derivative equal to the slope of\r                                 these points and solving for <em>x</em> produces the <em>c</em> value\r                                 that is considered the conclusion of the mean value theorem. Because\r                                 the coordinates are (0, 0) and (6, 0), the slope is 0. Setting the\r                                 derivative equal to zero (applying Rolle’s theorem) and solving for\r                                     <em>x</em> produces the following.</p> <p><img src=\"images/2dc3d0cd9f9c46ebad1a328ebd72fdba.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>(C) looks very good.\r                                 However, the correct answer is (B), 4 only, because the\r                                 <em>c</em>-value must be inside the given domain, also known as\r                                 “between the endpoints”. In this case, <em>x</em> = 0 does not\r                                 constitute a <em>c</em>-value because it is an endpoint of the given\r                                 domain.</p>"
      },

        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-6-q23",

        "question": "<p>Let <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) be\r                             the function defined by <img src=\"images/4b88d307b44d4918ac62b1fb5723ceea.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. On which of the following intervals is the graph of <em>y</em> =\r                                 <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) concave up?</p>",
        "options": [
          "(1, 2) only",
          "(–∞, 1) and (2, ∞)",

          "(2, ∞) only"
        ],

        "explanation": "<strong>B</strong> <p>To analyze concavity,\r                                 take the second derivative of <em>y</em>. The first derivative relies\r                                 on the fundamental theorem, and the second derivative uses the power\r                                 rule.</p> <p><img src=\"images/56085659d55545cc8a07d8885b26a2b2.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>For <em>y</em> to be\r                                 concave up, the second derivative must be positive. Set the second\r                                 derivative equal to 0, and solve to locate the critical values.</p> <p><img src=\"images/f91dc99ea7ae499393530a6d94243272.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>You could use test\r                                 intervals of (–∞, 1), (1, 2), and (2, ∞) to determine where the\r                                 second derivative is positive. Alternatively, you could recognize\r                                 that this is an upward-opening parabola, which tells you it must be\r                                 above the axis on the intervals in (B). Therefore, <em>y</em> =\r                                     <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) is concave up on the intervals (–∞, 1) and\r                                 (2, ∞).</p> <p>Hence, (B) is correct.\r                                 (A) is the interval where <em>y</em> is concave down. (D) is one of\r                                 the correct intervals, but the other interval is missing.</p>"

        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<strong>A</strong> <p>This integral needs to\r                                 be split into the sum of different integrals in order to evaluate it\r                                 correctly. If <em>x</em> = 7, then <img src=\"images/0b87ebedef834e01a2e369446e82c27c.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">.</p> <p><img src=\"images/b39c0b384364410d9afb0beee1f38608.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p><img src=\"images/acb8834602804852afecb88b6cf3f422.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Add this to the results\r                                 from the other integrals you split from the original. Then simplify.\r                                 Remember that <em>C </em>stands for an unknown constant in each\r                                 expression. So you can add <em>C</em><sub>1</sub><em> </em>+\r                                     <em>C</em><sub>2</sub><em> </em>+ <em>C</em><sub>3</sub> to get\r                                     <em>C</em>.</p> <p><img src=\"images/ba02c8520ec54e96aff8390044833eed.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Thus, (A) is correct.\r                                 (B) is not the answer because it incorrectly has the exponent of 3\r                                 on the (<em>x</em> + 7) binomial. (C) and (D) neglect to use the chain\r                                 rule and <em>u</em>-substitution when evaluating <img src=\"images/f0079a689f1648578963c9021e490968.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. Remember that <img src=\"images/15bad85244ad408a9f071b30aa65dcc1.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">.</p>"

        "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",
        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "<p>A particle moves along the\r                                 <em>x</em>-axis so that at time <em>t</em> ≥ 0, the acceleration of the\r                             particle is <img src=\"images/b9f1ccad7dcf4529ab5c000a4f645169.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. The position of the particle is 16 at <em>t</em> = 0, and the\r                             position of the particle is 9 at <em>t </em>= 1. What is the velocity at\r                                 <em>t</em> = 0 ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "–15",
          "9",
          "15",
          "30"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<strong>A</strong> <p>Because the acceleration\r                                 function is given, you must first take the antiderivative to get the\r                                 velocity function. Once you have the velocity function, take another\r                                 antiderivative to get the position function. Remember to add a\r                                 constant “+ <em>C</em>” whenever you take an antiderivative. Because\r                                     <img src=\"images/f0a9ab515649489abe751cfbc6888245.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, rewrite it as <img src=\"images/7a48fa86aaba4cfca0e55e778d1e5e52.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. Integrating both sides produces <img src=\"images/4fd99610423a4ee99aa41df1349e7877.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. The given information was with regard to position, so you\r                                 must integrate again. Do not use the same constant “+ <em>C</em>.”\r                                 Integrating both sides using a different constant produces <img src=\"images/2f9fb64d99514cb49f150b508c676fb2.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. The position at <em>t</em> = 0 was given as 16. Substituting\r                                     <em>t</em> = 0 and <em>x</em>(<em>t</em>) = 16 into the position\r                                 function gives the constant <em>B</em>, which must equal to 16. Using\r                                     <img src=\"images/091c5e41631647ad97bd20584ceeefba.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> and the position of the particle at <em>t </em>= 1 allows you\r                                 to solve for <em>C</em>. The position at <em>t</em> = 1 was given as 9.\r                                 When you substitute <em>t</em> = 1 and <em>x</em>(<em>t</em>) = 9 into the\r                                 position function, the constant <em>C</em> equals –15. The question is\r                                 asking for <em>v</em>(0). Because <img src=\"images/e7740534a0bc4476953ec8dfe9ce7f28.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, <em>v</em>(0) = –15.</p> <p>Therefore, (A) is\r                                 correct. (B) is <em>x</em>(1). (C) is the result when you solve for\r                                     <em>C</em> incorrectly. (D) is <em>a</em>(1).</p>"

Use the area formula to find the net\r                                 change.</p> <p><img src=\"images/189c7a4f84d147bc81efb04d05f17c1b.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>To find <em>f</em>(6), add\r                                 this net change to <em>f</em>(0).</p> <p><img src=\"images/4f1eb4199c794d329af691b15f20798d.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Hence, (D) is correct.\r                                 B) is the net change ignoring the original <em>f</em>(0).         "topic": "Section I: Part A (No Calculator)",

        "question": "<p>If <img src=\"images/4344ee59266d48d989ff49d367ff2954.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, then <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) is concave down on the interval</p>",

        "explanation": "<strong>D</strong> <p>A function,\r                                     <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>), is concave down when the second derivative\r                                 is negative. The following shows\r                                     individual integrals being used.</p> <p><img src=\"images/4a89c67d3eb1414385296e5f90f1869e.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>This equation shows\r                                     one integral being used.</p> <p><img src=\"images/ef4bdf10b49f47dcbfb466bc3a8a1f3c.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Hence, (C) is\r                                     correct. (D) does not use the\r                                     necessary <img src=\"images/d628ef7920c44501aa44dfe6c6b29d91.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">.         "question": "<p>The first derivative of\r                                 the function <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) is given by\r                                     <em>f</em><em>′</em>(<em>x</em>) = –<em>x</em> + 6<em>e</em><sup>cos\r                                         <em>x</em></sup>. Be careful because the 9th-degree term is less than the\r                                     given amount of <img src=\"images/66b9ce86476b405c8cedeafc7b99bcb9.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. So the polynomial that guarantees <img src=\"images/7d5e916fdf984820a4d0d285167048fc.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> is a polynomial of degree 7, which is the previous term\r                                     in the alternating series.</p> <p>Therefore, (D) is\r                                     correct.         "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<strong>B</strong>  <p>First differentiate\r                                     each side of the equation with respect to <em>x</em>. Remember to\r                                     use the product rule when differentiating –27.6<em>xy</em>.</p> <p><img src=\"images/18f8f2cb25bc4da2a16946018b35e3f1.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Recognize that to\r                                     have a horizontal tangent line, the derivative must equal 0.\r                                     Solve for <em>y </em>by cross-multiplying and simplifying.</p> <p><img src=\"images/648228acb8a74e6eb248bf91aa2a0c12.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Substitute this\r                                         <em>y</em>-value back into the original equation to find the\r                                     corresponding <em>x</em>-values.</p> <p><img src=\"images/ac344f7020cd417eae57df9f2380074e.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Enter this into your\r                                     ulator. Be extremely careful about the parenthesis. Use the\r                                     ulate Zero function to find when the graph crosses the\r                                     <em>x</em>-axis. Therefore, (B) is correct.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-6-q41",
        "topic": "Section I: Part B (Calculator Active)",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p>Given the function <img src=\"images/522b62e158414f4cb7abe60225d624a8.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"> for <em>x</em> > 0, which statement is true about the\r                                 approximation for <em>g</em>(14) using Euler’s method with step sizes\r                                 of 5 starting at <em>x</em> = 4 ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "The approximation is\r                             greater than <em>g</em>(14).",
          "The approximation is less\r                             than <em>g</em>(14).",
          "Using the coordinates (4,\r                             2), the first <img src=\"images/a2c60cb88620423884985d7e194230fd.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">.",
          "For approximating\r                                 <em>g</em>(<em>x</em>), the <em>y</em>-coordinate is used to find\r                                 ∆<em>y</em>."
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<strong>A</strong>  <p>To answer this\r                                     question, you must realize that Euler’s method is based on small\r                                     steps in the tangent line approximations to reach an\r                                     approximation for a particular <em>x</em>-value. The function is\r                                     given as <img src=\"images/a3d99cf508ce4d27ac240832e8badfd4.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, so the derivative is <img src=\"images/8856ac6d1b0740208498f9cbb19f461b.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. At the first coordinate of <em>x</em> = 4 the point (4,\r                                     2) is on the curve. Find its derivative.</p> <p><img src=\"images/de5f742634924c1eaf0b0d612d314f48.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>So the approximation\r                                     for <em>x</em> = 9 is <img src=\"images/ab4975a6edef4f72b6a09770cd7f6593.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. ulate the next value.</p> <p><img src=\"images/8e18662dd9f54036aa0effe43def5d81.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>So the approximation\r                                     for <em>x</em> = 14 is <img src=\"images/24c99a192de643b98889892cd9d3babe.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. Because <img src=\"images/63fdf3e4eda24817bb4df01c97fa1b7d.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, the approximation for <em>g</em>(14) is greater than\r                                         <em>g</em>(14). Because the function is strictly concave down\r                                     (its second derivative is less than 0) tangent line\r                                     approximation or, in this case, the result from Euler’s method\r                                     is greater than the actual <em>y</em>-coordinate of the function.</p> <p>Hence, (A) is\r                                     correct. (C) is incorrect as <img src=\"images/d90f306ec9ae428bba26fb6dbb12d4c1.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">. (D) is incorrect because the derivative is strictly\r                                     defined by the <em>x</em>-coordinates in this case, not the\r                                         <em>y</em>-coordinates.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-6-q42",
        "topic": "Section I: Part B (Calculator Active)",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p>The position of a\r                                 particle moving in the <em>xy</em>-plane is given by the parametric\r                                 equations <em>x</em>(<em>t</em>) = sin (3<sup><em>t</em></sup>) and\r                                     <em>y</em>(<em>t</em>) = cos (3<sup><em>t</em></sup>) for time\r                                     <em>t</em> ≥ 0. What is the speed of the particle at <em>t</em> =\r                                 2.7 ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "0.640",
          "1",
          "2.542",
          "21.332"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<strong>D</strong>  <p>The speed of a\r                                     parametric function is the absolute value of the velocity.\r                                     However, because the velocity is a vector having a magnitude and\r                                     direction, you must use the following formula.</p> <p><img src=\"images/b6ad45fcded24c6880e756eefd047fc9.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>You should\r                                     definitely use your ulator. Be sure to type the functions\r                                     correctly and have your ulator in radian mode. The derivatives\r                                     should be found in the ulator as well, using the numerical\r                                     derivative button for an equation when <em>x</em> = <em>x</em>.</p>  <img src=\"images/chapter30_a-102_103.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">  <p>The speed of the\r                                     particle is 21.332.</p> <p>Thus, (D) is\r                                     correct. (A) is the absolute value of the velocity quotients but\r                                     is not the speed in parametric motion. (B) evaluates the\r                                     position functions incorrectly in the speed formula. (C)\r                                     neglects to square the derivatives in the formula.</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-6-q43",
        "topic": "Section I: Part B (Calculator Active)",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p>A polynomial\r                                     <em>p</em>(<em>x</em>) has a relative minimum at (–3, 1), a relative\r                                 maximum at (1, 4), a relative minimum at (4, –2), and no other\r                                 critical points. How many zeros does <em>p</em>(<em>x</em>) have?</p>",
        "options": [
          "1",
          "2",
          "3",
          "4"
        ],
        "answer": "B",
        "explanation": "<strong>B</strong>  <p>The fact that\r                                         <em>p</em>(<em>x</em>) is a polynomial tells you that its graph\r                                     is continuous everywhere. Because the first local minimum is\r                                     above the <em>x</em>-axis, that point does not cause zeros. The\r                                     local maximum point also does not cause any zeros due to its\r                                     location. The second minimum is located below the axis, which\r                                     means the graph must go through zero to reach the minimum.\r                                     Because that point is a local minimum and there are no other\r                                     critical points, the graph turns back up after (4, –2). This\r                                     forces the graph to go back through the <em>x</em>-axis, creating\r                                     a second zero.</p> <p>You could plot these\r                                     points in your ulator and connect the dots to see that there\r                                     will be two zeros.</p> <p>Thus, (B) is\r                                     correct. (A) gets you to the second minimum but does not account\r                                     for the graph turning back up. (C) is the number of zeros for\r                                         <em>f′</em>(<em>x</em>).</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-6-q44",
        "topic": "Section I: Part B (Calculator Active)",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p>What is the\r                                 <em>x</em>-intercept of the tangent line to the function\r                                     <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>) = <em>e<sup>x</sup></em> + 3 at <em>x</em> = 1\r                                 ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "–1.104",
          "1.104",
          "3",
          "5.350"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "<strong>A</strong>  <p>First find the\r                                     equation of the tangent line, <em>y</em> – (<em>e</em> + 3) =\r                                         <em>e</em>(<em>x</em> – 1). Solve for <em>y</em> and enter this\r                                     into your ulator. Use the ulate Zero function to find the\r                                         solution <img src=\"images/c5829e6713e7483c93516412a59265a5.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, (A).</p>"
      },
      {
        "id": "ap-mock-calcbc-full-6-q45",
        "topic": "Section I: Part B (Calculator Active)",
        "difficulty": "hard",
        "question": "<p>If the derivative of\r                                 function <em>f</em> is defined as <em>f</em><em>′</em>(<em>x</em>) =\r                                     4<em>x</em><sup>3</sup> – 6<em>x</em><sup>2</sup> + 6 and if\r                                     <em>f</em>(1) = 7.158, which of the following is <em>f</em>(3.5)\r                                 ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "2.185",
          "31",
          "85.313",
          "87.471"
        ],
        "answer": "D",
        "explanation": "<strong>D</strong>  <p>Because\r                                         <em>f'</em>(<em>x</em>) is given, the antiderivative must be\r                                     taken using the power rule to find <em>f</em>(<em>x</em>). The power\r                                     rule involves increasing the exponent by 1 and then dividing the\r                                     coefficient by the new exponent. Don’t forget to include a\r                                     constant of integration whenever taking the antiderivative of a\r                                     function.</p> <p><img src=\"images/8fef61c26ab34efc82f96cfabce45ef7.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Using the given\r                                     value <em>f</em>(1) = 7.158, you can determine the constant,\r                                         <em>C</em>.</p> <p><img src=\"images/0b81490f636c4e65830e191e5a63dc51.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Now substitute 3.5\r                                     into the antiderivative. Use the ulator's ulate Value function\r                                     for fast ulations.<img src=\"images/06e31263b39f40878ea3cd6840a98b78.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">, to get  <em>f</em>(3.5) = 87.471.</p> <p>Hence, (D) is\r                                     correct. (B) is <em>f'</em>(2.5), and (C) is the result if you\r                                     forget to include the constant, (A) in your antiderivative\r                                     constant.</p>"
      }
    ]
  },

          "<img src=\"images/e9a2e40f3b9c415aa6754c6b1842f159.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",
          "12 – <em>$\\pi$</em>",

          "24"

Don’t forget to use the chain rule when taking\r                                 the derivative of the second term:</p> <p><img src=\"images/30fd954c4fbd497497b6c1a0f9d50f6d.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\"></p> <p>Thus, (B) is\r                                 correct.</p>"

        "question": "<p>Which of\r                             the following is a necessary and sufficient condition for a\r                             function <em>f</em> to be continuous at <em>x</em> = 4 ?</p>",
        "options": [
          "<img src=\"images/00daa9230ea04a52971f3f439f912fd6.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">\r                             exists.",
          "<em>f</em> is differentiable\r                             at <em>x</em> = 4.",
          "<em>f</em>(4) exists.",
          "<img src=\"images/d2680258285841eaba0b61a0669fc0e2.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">."

        "explanation": "<strong>D</strong> \r                             This question is testing your understanding of what it means for a\r                             function to be continuous at a point, in terms of limits. In other words, the correct\r                             answer is equivalent to the continuity of <em>f</em> at <em>x</em> = 4. Because differentiability at a\r                             point is a stronger condition than continuity at a point, (B) can be\r                             eliminated. (C) is certainly implied by the continuity of <em>f</em> at\r                                 <em>x</em> = 4, but it is not enough to\r                             imply continuity, so it may also be eliminated.         "topic": "Parametric & Polar",

        "question": "<p>A\r                             self-storage company wants to construct a rectangular storage unit\r                             with a base length\r                             3 times the base width.         "topic": "Parametric & Polar",

        "question": "<p>An\r                             equivalent representation of the definite integral\r                             <img src=\"images/6898c3d49e3c46b6b11d43edbd520f52.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">\r                             is</p>",

          "<img src=\"images/dc8f2f66393047f6b61e2f1d8da45f2a.png\" class=\"exam-img\" style=\"max-width:100%; vertical-align:middle; margin:4px 0;\">",

        ],

        "explanation": "<strong>C</strong> \r                             This is an exercise in the correct application of <em>u</em>-substitution\r                             in a definite integral. Plug the original limits for <em>x</em> into the expression\r                                 <em>u</em> = <em>x </em><sup>2</sup> to\r                             get the new limits, 1 and 9, and the correct answer follows, which is\r                             (C)."

          "1 + 2x + 4x^2 + 8x^3",
          "1 + x + \\frac{x^2}{2} + \\frac{x^3}{6}",
          "2x + 2x^2 + \\frac{4}{3}x^3",
          "1 + 2x + x^2 + \\frac{1}{3}x^3"
        ],
        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "e^u = 1 + u + u^2/2! + u^3/3! + ... Substituting u = 2x gives 1 + 2x + (2x)^2/2 + (2x)^3/6 = 1 + 2x + 2x^2 + (4/3)x^3."

        "difficulty": "medium",
        "question": "Find the radius of convergence R for the power series \\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} \\frac{(x - 3)^n}{n \\cdot 5^n}.",
        "options": [
          "1",
          "3",
          "5",
          "\\infty",
          "0"
        ],
        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "Use Ratio Test: \\lim_{n \\to \\infty} |\\frac{(x-3)^{n+1}}{(n+1)5^{n+1}} \\cdot \\frac{n 5^n}{(x-3)^n}| = \\frac{|x-3|}{5} < 1 \\implies |x - 3| < 5. Thus, R = 5."

        "question": "If f(2) = 3, f'(2) = -1, f''(2) = 4, and f'''(2) = -12, what is the coefficient of (x - 2)^3 in the Taylor series for f centered at x = 2?",

          "-12",

          "4",

        "answer": "C",
        "explanation": "The coefficient of (x - a)^n is f^{(n)}(a)/n!. For n = 3: f'''(2)/3! = -12 / 6 = -2."
      },

          "\\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty} (-1)^n \\frac{x^{2n+2}}{(2n)!}"

        "answer": "A",
        "explanation": "\\cos(u) = \\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty} (-1)^n u^{2n}/(2n)!. Substituting u = x^2 yields \\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty} (-1)^n (x^2)^{2n}/(2n)! = \\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty} (-1)^n x^{4n}/(2n)!."
